articles.title: Ghost Rovers: I Called 12 Machines NASA Left Behind. One Picked Up.
articles.description: A 1969 Mission Control console for kids. Built in one day for NASA Space Apps 2026.   TL;DR: For NASA...
articles.body_html:
A 1969 Mission Control console for kids. Built in one day for NASA Space Apps 2026.

TL;DR: For NASA Space Apps 2026 I built Ghost Rovers, a free web app where kids sit at a 1969 Mission Control console and call the 12 machines NASA left on the Moon and Mars. Five Moon machines answer NO SIGNAL, the Apollo 11 Laser Mirror answers, and Mars stays quiet. I directed it in one day, with Claude planning and checking and Google Antigravity building, and every fact traces back to NASA's own records.

The first commit went in at 10:47 a.m. PST on Saturday: a 15-minute test to see whether my phone could spin a 3D Moon without choking. At 7:32 p.m. I clicked Submit for Judging. In between, the project grew a second planet, a study kit for teachers, a 27-second demo video with Apollo radio beeps, and one correction I'm glad I asked for.

NASA Space Apps is NASA's global hackathon, run over one weekend. This year one of the challenges was called Abandoned but not Forgotten: tell the story of the hardware NASA has left on the Moon and Mars, for school-age space fans. The challenge text even suggested "an interactive map of the Moon with clickable ghost rovers." I didn't have to look any further.

Why this one? I love helping people, teaching people, and learning. Kids hear about rockets launching. They almost never hear about what stayed behind. The facts all exist in NASA's catalog, but they read like a spec sheet: catalog IDs, coordinates, mass budgets. Nobody tells a 9-year-old that a car has been parked on the Moon since before their grandparents had cell phones. lol

earlgreyhot1701D / ghost-rovers

Ghost Rovers

12 machines are still on the Moon and Mars. Only 1 still answers.

A 1969 Mission Control console where kids ages 8 to 12 radio the hardware NASA left behind, on the Moon and on Mars.

Play it live · Watch the 27-second demo · Slides (PDF) · Go to Mars · Study notebook · Fact check · SI disclosure

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 · Abandoned but not Forgotten · Team Clew Labs (La Shara Cordero)

The problem

Kids hear about rockets launching. They almost never hear about what stayed behind. The facts are all in NASA's catalog, but they read like a spec sheet: COSPAR IDs, coordinates, mass budgets. Nobody tells a 9-year-old that a car has been parked on the Moon since before their grandparents had cell phones.

What Ghost Rovers does

You sit at a Mission Control console. Six machines are out there. You…

View on GitHub

Pick one. Press CALL GHOST.

You sit at a Mission Control console. Six machines are out there on the Moon. You pick one and press CALL GHOST. Radio static. Then:

On the Moon Today
Surveyor 3 Quiet since 1967
Apollo 11 Laser Mirror Still answers
Eagle's launch pad Resting since 1969
Apollo 12 moonquake station Switched off 1977
Apollo 15 Rover Parked since 1971
Apollo 17 Rover Parked since 1972

Five reply NO SIGNAL with the year they went quiet. One answers. Scientists on Earth still bounce lasers off the Apollo 11 mirror, so the console draws a beam from Earth to the Moon and back, and the round trip takes 2.5 seconds, the real number.

Press M and the console flips to Mars: Viking 1 and 2, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, and InSight. None of them answer. Yet.

Each machine has a file: its original mission, a short story in its own voice, three questions kids ask ("Could I drive it?" "What's it made of?"), its real NASA photo, and a live counter of how long it has been sitting there, down to the second. READ TO ME reads the file out loud. Call all six on a world and you earn a Junior Flight Controller badge you can save.

The console had to look like 1969

I spent the first real block of the day on design, before any build. Claude mocked up three directions: Museum After Dark, Field Notebook, and Mission Control 1969. I picked Mission Control, then sent the first version back because it didn't look enough like 1969. The second pass got the details: amber clocks, a red label-maker tape, a curved wall screen, console sounds generated in code instead of recorded.

Then I wrote one rule into the agent's instructions before it built anything: the design is like-for-like. Build what was approved. If you have an improvement, list it separately and don't build it until I say yes. I've had agents "clean up" a design into something generic before, and I wasn't going to spend the afternoon arguing with a button radius.

Every fact had to survive NSSDCA

NSSDCA, NASA's Space Science Data Coordinated Archive, keeps a record for every mission. Every date, landing site, and status in Ghost Rovers was checked line by line against those records, and both fact-check logs are public in the repo.

The check caught real overclaims. A draft called the Apollo 15 rover "the first car on the Moon." The Soviet Union's robot rover, Lunokhod 1, got there in 1970, a year earlier. The line now reads "the first car astronauts drove on the Moon." That kind of fix is small on screen and it's the whole difference between a fun app and a fun app a teacher can trust.

The same rule applied to the Mars clock. "Light time Earth to Mars: 3 to 22 minutes" comes from NASA's Mars fact sheet: the closest and farthest Earth distances, divided by the speed of light.

Two agents, one notebook, one rule

I don't write the code. I direct, the agents generate, I check and decide. Here's who did what on Saturday:

Who What they did
Me The idea, the kid audience, the 1969 look, every design call, every yes or no
Claude (Opus 5.5) The plan, design mockups, fact checks against NSSDCA, an independent check after every block, the docs, the demo video and slides
Google Antigravity Built the site in small blocks: propose a plan, wait for my approval, then build
Google's Gemini Notebook A public study notebook from the same NASA sources: a quiz, flashcards, and a mind map for each world, plus a podcast with AI voices

The rhythm worked. Antigravity proposed, I approved, it built, Claude checked the result in a real browser at three screen sizes and ran an accessibility scan, and only then did the next block start. Claude's checks caught things that read fine in code and looked wrong on screen: the Earth sitting inside the Moon during the laser animation, a badge title clipped off the edge, an answer box covering the story text.

The friction was mostly plumbing. Antigravity's built-in browser couldn't take screenshots on my machine, so it switched to a headless script. Old editor tabs kept trying to save stale copies of files over new ones. Once I learned to close the tab and pick Don't Save, that stopped.

Space Apps calls AI tools "Super Intelligence," or SI, and asks you to label anything SI made. So every code file has a one-line SI header, every SI-assisted image and video carries a visible label, and the repo has a full disclosure log of what each tool did.

The rule was in the wrong file

Around 4 p.m., Claude ran a code review and pointed out that main.js was 1,104 lines and main.css was 2,775. I loathe god files. My build rules say one file, one job.

Then we found out why. The rule lived in the file Claude reads. It never made it into the file Antigravity reads on every block. So Antigravity did the reasonable thing and kept adding each new feature to the files that already existed, block after block, and Claude's checks were looking at whether things worked, not at how big the files were getting.

We split the CSS into nine files, all under 500 lines, and proved the split changed nothing: the joined files match the original line for line, and before and after screenshots at three screen sizes came out identical. The two big JavaScript files stay as they are until after the hackathon. Each one is a single giant function, and splitting that the night before a deadline is how you break the thing judges are about to open. They're listed in the agent instructions now as known exceptions, with a 500-line rule for everything else.

"Yet" needed a meaning

By 7 p.m. I was writing the project description, and something in my own pitch bugged me. Mars: none of them answer. Yet. What do we do with "yet"?

That question turned up a mistake. Claude's draft of the description said no machine on Mars answers. That isn't true. Curiosity has been driving around Gale Crater since 2012, and Perseverance has been working in Jezero Crater since 2021. In October, Perseverance broke Opportunity's off-world driving record. The six machines in Ghost Rovers are quiet. Mars is not.

My first instinct was to make Curiosity and Perseverance callable, like the Laser Mirror. Claude advised against it, and I agreed: the challenge is about discarded equipment, and those two are working missions with teams driving them every day. Calling them ghosts would stretch the theme and break "only 1 still answers" everywhere at once.

So they became the answer to "yet" instead. Finish the Mars check, and the badge panel adds one more row:

Antigravity usage was running low by then, so Claude built that row itself, as a new file with one job so the big files stayed untouched, and Antigravity committed it. The Mars clock already said "People on Mars: none yet," so "yet" ended up meaning what it should have meant all along: nobody has visited these machines. The next voice from those landing sites could be a kid watching today.

Thirty seconds, with Apollo radio beeps

The demo had to be 30 seconds or less, so Claude built a 27-second film in the app's own look: the console powering on, the Laser Mirror call, the switch to Mars, and a closing card with the classroom kit.

The sound is my favorite part. Claude logged every sound the app made while a script played it, the clicks, the static, the laser ping, the NO SIGNAL buzz, and rebuilt them at the exact moments they happened. I asked for more Mission Control, so it added Quindar tones, the short beeps you hear on Apollo-era Mission Control radio audio. The narration is a synthetic voice, labeled on screen and in the file. The video is on YouTube.

The form fought back

The last bug of the day wasn't in the app. Claude filled in 15 NASA data links on the submission form by typing them, and a check afterward found the typing had dropped letters: display.ction instead of display.action, in several URLs. It reset all 15 and checked them again. Later, a second editor tab I'd left open almost saved an older, emptier version over the finished one. Reload, don't save. Lesson learned twice in one evening.

What it can't do

  • No human voice yet. A real Mission Control voice, ghost names, and Spanish are the v2 list.
  • The podcast covers the Moon only.
  • Two JavaScript files are still far over my own 500-line rule.
  • Phone and tablet checks ran in browser emulation, not on every real device. I tested on my own Android phone.
  • Twelve machines is a start. NASA has left a lot more out there.

Try it

Play Ghost Rovers, or go straight to Mars. Keys 1 to 6 pick a machine, C calls it, M flips worlds. No login, no tracking, no data collected.

For teachers: the study notebook has a quiz, flashcards, and a mind map for each world, and it's public.

The numbers, from the repo on submission day:
Machines 12 (6 Moon, 6 Mars)
Answering 1 (plus 2 working rovers linked on Mars)
Accessibility scan (axe-core, WCAG 2.1 AA) 0 violations on both worlds
First commit to submit 10:47 a.m. to 7:32 p.m.
Commits by submission 21

Space Apps sent me a participant certificate that says Galactic Problem Solver. That one's going on the wall.

Did a machine answer when you called it? I'd love to hear which one you tried first.

Quick context if you are new here. I work in the California courts, running court operations for the county. I started building with AI in July 2025 and I have been learning in public ever since. I don't write the code. I direct, the agents generate, I validate and decide. I build the Clew Suite, a set of civic tech tools for making complex systems easier to inspect.

Built with AI assistance in November 2026. NASA facts link to NASA's own records, and the fact-check logs are in the repo. These tools move fast, so check the source before you quote me.

AI Assisted. Human Approved. Powered by NLP.

articles.title: Tips to Work on Your Side Project While Working Full-Time
articles.description: Here's a scene you might know.  It's 8:40 PM. Dinner is done. You open your laptop to finally work on...
articles.body_html:
Here's a scene you might know.

It's 8:40 PM. Dinner is done. You open your laptop to finally work on your side project, and you read the same function three times without understanding it. So you check one tab. Then another. At 10:15 you close the laptop, tired and a little annoyed at yourself.

Nothing is wrong with you. You spent the whole day using your brain for your job, and now you want to use the same brain again. Most side project advice pretends you have a spare one in a drawer. "Wake up at 5 AM." "Grind every night." Sure.

This post goes the other way. Smaller steps, slower pace, and something you can still be doing six months from now. Some of it won't fit your life exactly, and that's fine. Take what works, skip what doesn't, and feel free to disagree with me. 😄

Reading time: about 10 minutes


TL;DR
  • Count your real free hours, then plan for those.
  • Pick one project and keep every weekly goal small.
  • Cut tasks until one fits in a single session.
  • Match the work to your energy, and protect your sleep.
  • Rest days are part of the plan, not a failure of it.

In this post
  • Count the Hours You Really Have
  • Pick One Project. Really, Just One.
  • Make the Weekly Goal Almost Embarrassingly Small
  • Cut Big Tasks Until They Fit One Evening
  • Build a Routine That Survives a Bad Week
  • Your Energy Matters More Than Your Hours
  • Make Distractions Annoying to Reach
  • When the Excitement Wears Off
  • When Progress Feels Painfully Slow
  • Don't Let It Eat the Rest of Your Life
  • A Simple Plan for This Week
  • Quick Reference

Count the Hours You Really Have

Most of us guess. "I'll code every evening" sounds great on Sunday and falls apart by Wednesday.

So try this once. Take a normal week and mark the hours that are truly free. Not the ones you'd like to have. Subtract the commute, cooking, chores, the family time you don't want to cut, and the evenings when your brain is already done.

For a lot of people with a full-time job, the honest answer looks something like this:

  • Three short sessions on weekdays, about 45 to 60 minutes each
  • One longer session on the weekend, maybe two or three hours

That's roughly 5 to 8 hours a week. It sounds tiny. It isn't. Plenty of real projects have been built in "tiny" hours, as long as nobody wastes them deciding what to do.

Plan for the number you actually have. A plan for the life you wish you had is just a nice document.

Pick One Project. Really, Just One.

This is where most side projects quietly die.

You start an app. Two weeks later, you get a better idea, so you start that one too. Now you have a folder with five repos, and none of them can be shown to another human being.

When your time is limited, splitting it is the fastest way to finish nothing. So pick one. A few questions can help you choose:

  • Would you still care about this in three months?
  • Can you get a first rough version done in weeks, not years?
  • Will you learn something you want to learn anyway?

The other ideas aren't dead. Put them in a notes file called later.md and leave them there. When the current project is done, or when you stop it on purpose, you can open that file and pick the next one.

Make the Weekly Goal Almost Embarrassingly Small

"Build the app" is not a goal. It's a mountain, and your brain knows it. That's why you feel resistance before you even sit down.

A weekly goal should fit in your real hours with some room left over. Something like:

  • Set up the project and get a login page showing on screen
  • Build the form that saves a new entry
  • Fix the three annoying bugs and put it online

Pick one or two. Write them where you'll see them. On Sunday, look at what got done and choose the next ones.

Here's the part nobody likes to hear: estimate how long it will take, then double it. Seriously. Small things grow, especially when you're tired. If the goal still feels good at twice the time, keep it. If not, make it smaller. 😅

Also decide what "done" means before you start. "Learn React" never ends. "Build a to-do page with add, delete, and a saved list" does.

Copy-paste weekly goal template 
## Week of <date>

**Goal 1:** small enough to finish in one or two sessions
**Goal 2:** optional

**Done means:** one sentence
**Next step:** one line

## Later
- idea
- another idea

Cut Big Tasks Until They Fit One Evening

A good rule: every task on your list should be finishable in one sitting. If it can't, it's still too big.

Say your task is "Add user accounts." That could swallow a month. Slice it:

  1. Create the users table
  2. Build the sign-up form
  3. Save the new user
  4. Build the login form
  5. Check the password and start a session
  6. Lock the pages that need a login

Now each piece is an evening. You never have to wonder what to do next, and that matters a lot when you only have an hour.

One small habit helps more than it should. Before you stop for the day, write one line about what comes next. Something like this:

NEXT: connect the login form to the API
STUCK ON: session cookie not saving

Tomorrow you skip the "where was I?" fog and just start.

Build a Routine That Survives a Bad Week

Motivation comes and goes. A routine doesn't need it. It just needs a time and a place.

Here are two schedules you can steal and bend:

Morning people Evening people
Weekdays Mon, Wed, Fri: 6:30 to 7:30 AM Tue, Thu: 8:30 to 9:30 PM, after dinner has settled
Weekend Sat: 9:00 to 11:30 AM Sun: 2:00 to 4:30 PM
Everything else Not project time Not project time

These times are examples. Shift them to fit your own days.

Look at how much empty space is in there. That's on purpose. Rest days are part of the plan. Three or four sessions that actually happen beat seven that live only in your head.

Tip: make starting easy. Leave the editor open to the right file, keep your next step written down, and keep the setup friction low. The harder it is to begin, the more likely you'll skip it. Some days the hardest part of the whole project is opening the laptop.

Your Energy Matters More Than Your Hours

Two free hours don't help if your head is empty. After a day of coding, your brain can be as tired as your legs after a long walk. A few things that make this easier:

Put a gap between work and project time

Eat, take a short walk, sit somewhere without a screen for 20 minutes. Jumping straight from the work laptop to the project laptop rarely goes well. ☕

Match the task to your energy

The cheat sheet below shows how.

Allow a tiny version of a session

On a bad night, promise yourself 20 minutes. If you keep going, great. If not, you still showed up, and the habit stays alive.


Your energy Good project tasks
Sharp Design choices, weird bugs, anything that needs real thinking
Okay Building features you already planned, writing tests
Tired Renaming things, writing the README, testing what you built, tidying code

No row here is "better". The goal is a task that fits the brain you have tonight.

And sometimes the right move is to skip the session and go to bed. That's not failing. Code written at 1 AM usually gets rewritten the next day anyway. 😴

Make Distractions Annoying to Reach

Don't fight distractions during the session. Set things up before you sit down, because willpower runs out fast.

  • Put the phone in another room, or at least on Do Not Disturb
  • Close work chat, email, and every tab that isn't for this project
  • Know your task before you start, so you don't wander into "research" that lasts the whole hour

Watch out for one sneaky trap: endless setup. Choosing the perfect stack, the perfect folder structure, or the perfect task app can eat a full week and produce zero features. Use tools you already know. Boring is good here.

And when a shiny new idea shows up mid-session, write it in later.md and get back to work. It will still be shiny tomorrow.

When the Excitement Wears Off

At the start, everything is fun. Around the middle, it gets boring. That's normal, and it happens to nearly every project.

A few things that help:

  • Keep a short "done" list. Even one line per week. On days when you feel stuck, reading it reminds you that you're moving.
  • Get something working early. A rough version that does one thing is far more exciting than a perfect plan.
  • Show it to one person. A friend, a coworker, an online group. You don't need an audience. You need one person who says "oh nice, what's next?"
  • Remember why you started. Learning something? Building a tool you want? Maybe earning a bit on the side? Keep that reason where you can see it.

If you've truly stopped caring, be honest with yourself. Is the idea still worth it? Dropping a project on purpose is very different from letting it fade away and feeling guilty every time you see the folder. Both are allowed. The first one just feels a lot better. 🙂

When Progress Feels Painfully Slow

It will. You might spend a whole evening on one bug and close the laptop wondering what you even did. That's what working in small pieces feels like.

Some thoughts for those nights:

  • Five hours a week still adds up. It just doesn't feel like it day by day.
  • Don't compare yourself with people who seem to ship something new every Friday. You don't know their hours, their team, or what they leave out of the story.
  • Shrink the first version. Cut features until it's small enough to finish. You can always add more after someone actually uses it.
  • Once a month, open the project and compare it with how it looked four weeks ago. The gap is usually bigger than it feels.

Don't Let It Eat the Rest of Your Life

A side project should be something you chose. When it starts feeling like a second job with no salary and no days off, something has to change.

Warning signs worth taking seriously

  • You dread opening the project
  • You feel annoyed when someone invites you out
  • You're trading sleep for coding hours

  • You're tired all the time, even on days off

Limits that keep things healthy

  • Keep at least one full day a week with zero project work


  • Don't pay for coding hours with sleep. Ever.


  • Protect your meals, your exercise, and the people you care about


  • Don't code during family time or plans you already made

    • If you notice two or three of those warning signs, ease off. Cut the weekly goal in half, take a week away, or pause the project completely for a while. The code will wait. It's patient like that.

    Caution: every single commitment can look small and reasonable on its own. A little extra here, a quick favor there, a new goal because you suddenly feel good after one great night of sleep. Add them up and you're out of energy. So if you want to sprint, give the sprint a clear finish line and plan some rest after it.


    Your job, your health, and your people matter more than any side project. The project fits into your life, not the other way around.

    A Simple Plan for This Week

    If you want somewhere to start, here's the whole thing:

    1. Pick one project and write its name at the top of a notes file
    2. Count your real free hours for the next seven days
    3. Choose two small goals that fit those hours (then ask if they'd still fit at double the time)
    4. Put three sessions in your calendar like real appointments
    5. At the end of each session, write down the very next step

    That's it. No perfect system. Just a small start you can repeat.

    Quick Reference

    Bookmark this part for the nights when everything feels too big.

    If this happens Try this
    You never find time Count your real free hours, then plan for those
    Too many ideas Pick one project and park the rest in later.md
    The goal feels huge Shrink it, then double the time estimate
    The task feels huge Cut it until it fits one session
    You keep skipping sessions Fixed times, a ready editor, and a written next step
    Your brain is fried Take a gap, then do an easy task or a 20-minute version
    You keep getting distracted Phone away, tabs closed, task decided before you start
    Motivation drops Keep a "done" list and show it to one person
    Progress feels slow Compare with last month, not with other people
    You feel burned out Halve the goals, rest, and pause if you have to

    Last Thing

    Working on a side project next to a full-time job isn't about hustling harder than everyone else. It's about keeping the goals small, protecting your rest, and showing up often enough that the work piles up quietly.

    Some weeks will go well. Some won't. Both count. 🐞

    If this helped, send it to a developer friend with a half-finished project sitting in a folder. They might need the nudge.

    Now go close a tab or two. You've earned it. 🙌

articles.title: TypeScript `Type Predicates` on Arrays: Writing `filter` Calls That Actually Narrow the Element Type
articles.description: Array.filter() returns the original element type without type predicates. Learn how to write filter callbacks that actually narrow union types, null checks, and optional properties in TypeScript codebases.
articles.body_html:
TypeScript Type Predicates on Arrays: Writing filter Calls That Actually Narrow the Element Type

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Why Array.filter() Doesn't Narrow Types (And Why You Need Type Predicates)

TypeScript's control flow analysis narrows types brilliantly within an if block. Check for undefined, and the variable becomes non-nullable inside the branch. Test typeof x === "string", and TypeScript knows the value is a string. Developers who rely on this behavior in conditional logic often assume the same narrowing applies to Array.filter(). The compiler sees the predicate callback, sees the check inside it, and returns the narrowed type. That assumption breaks the moment the filtered array gets used.

array.filter returns original union type instead of narrowed type

The filtered array still has the original union type because TypeScript treats the filter callback as a boolean function. The type system does not infer that a true return means the element matches a specific type. Without an explicit type predicate, the compiler assumes nothing about the relationship between the callback result and the element type.

type predicate returns properly narrowed array type

Type predicates fix this by telling TypeScript that when the callback returns true, the element has a specific type. The value is Type syntax establishes a contract between the runtime check and the type system. The compiler narrows the array element type based on that contract.

Key Takeaways

  • Array.filter() returns the original element type without explicit type predicates, even when the callback performs runtime type checks.
  • Type predicates use value is Type syntax to tell TypeScript that a true return guarantees a specific type for the value.
  • TypeScript 5.5+ infers type predicates automatically for simple single-return callbacks, but complex logic still requires explicit annotations.
  • Type predicates carry "if and only if" semantics: true means the value has the type, false means it does not.
  • Truthiness checks (like !!x) do not infer type predicates for numbers because 0 is falsy but still a valid number.

Understanding Type Predicates: The value is Type Syntax

A type predicate is a return type annotation that connects a boolean result to a type assertion. The syntax parameterName is Type appears where a normal return type would go. When the function returns true, TypeScript narrows the parameter to the specified type. When the function returns false, TypeScript narrows the parameter to exclude that type.

The predicate establishes a bidirectional contract. The function author claims that a true result guarantees the type, and a false result guarantees the opposite. TypeScript enforces neither direction at compile time. The type predicate is a promise, not a proof.

function isString(value: unknown): value is string {
  return typeof value === "string";
}

const items: unknown[] = ["hello", 42, "world", null];
const strings = items.filter(isString);
// strings: string[]

The isString function returns value is string. When used in a filter callback, TypeScript sees that true means the element is a string, so the filtered array becomes string[]. Without the type predicate, the result would remain unknown[] because the compiler cannot infer what the check accomplishes.

Type predicates work with any type, including union types, intersection types, and custom interfaces. The predicate must reference a parameter name from the current function signature. Returning value is string when the parameter is named item will cause a compile error.

interface User {
  id: number;
  name: string;
}

interface Admin extends User {
  permissions: string[];
}

function isAdmin(user: User): user is Admin {
  return "permissions" in user;
}

const users: User[] = [
  { id: 1, name: "Alice" },
  { id: 2, name: "Bob", permissions: ["read", "write"] }
];

const admins = users.filter(isAdmin);
// admins: Admin[]

The isAdmin predicate narrows User to Admin by checking for the permissions property. The filter callback applies the predicate, and TypeScript narrows the result array to Admin[].

Type predicate syntax diagram

Writing Type Predicates for Common Filter Scenarios

Filtering null or undefined values is the most common use case for type predicates. Arrays with optional elements or nullable types require explicit narrowing to access properties safely downstream.

function isDefined<T>(value: T | null | undefined): value is T {
  return value != null;
}

const scores: (number | null)[] = [42, null, 88, null, 95];
const validScores = scores.filter(isDefined);
// validScores: number[]

const average = validScores.reduce((sum, score) => sum + score, 0) / validScores.length;

The isDefined predicate uses a generic type parameter to preserve the non-nullable type. The value != null check covers both null and undefined (loose equality). The filtered array becomes number[], and downstream operations like reduce work without type errors.

Union type filtering requires predicates that distinguish between the union members. The check must be discriminative enough to separate one type from the others.

type ApiResponse = 
  | { status: "success"; data: string }
  | { status: "error"; message: string };

function isSuccess(response: ApiResponse): response is { status: "success"; data: string } {
  return response.status === "success";
}

const responses: ApiResponse[] = [
  { status: "success", data: "result1" },
  { status: "error", message: "failed" },
  { status: "success", data: "result2" }
];

const successfulResults = responses.filter(isSuccess);
// successfulResults: { status: "success"; data: string }[]

successfulResults.forEach(result => {
  console.log(result.data); // no type error
});

The isSuccess predicate checks the status discriminant. When status === "success", TypeScript knows the response has a data property instead of a message property. The filtered array contains only successful responses.

Filtering by property existence works when union members have different shapes. The in operator checks for property presence and serves as the runtime check for the predicate.

interface Cat {
  meow(): void;
}

interface Dog {
  bark(): void;
}

function isCat(animal: Cat | Dog): animal is Cat {
  return "meow" in animal;
}

const animals: (Cat | Dog)[] = [
  { meow: () => console.log("meow") },
  { bark: () => console.log("woof") },
  { meow: () => console.log("purr") }
];

const cats = animals.filter(isCat);
cats.forEach(cat => cat.meow());

The isCat predicate uses the in operator to detect the meow method. The filtered array becomes Cat[], and calling meow() on each element is safe.

Type Predicates vs. Type Assertions: When Each Approach Fits

Type predicates and type assertions both force TypeScript to treat a value as a specific type, but predicates operate at function boundaries while assertions operate at expression sites.

Aspect Type Predicate Type Assertion
Syntax value is Type (return type) as Type (expression suffix)
Scope Affects caller scope after function returns true Affects only the immediate expression
Reusability Defined once, used everywhere the function is called Repeated at every usage site
Runtime check Backed by function body logic No runtime enforcement
Type narrowing propagation Persists through control flow Limited to the assertion expression
Compile-time safety None — predicate logic can lie None — assertion can be wrong

type predicate narrows caller scope vs type assertion narrows expression only

Type assertions work for one-off narrowing where a predicate function would be overkill. Casting a variable to a more specific type after a manual check fits this pattern.

const response: ApiResponse = await fetch("/api/data").then(r => r.json());

if (response.status === "success") {
  const data = (response as { status: "success"; data: string }).data;
  console.log(data);
}

The assertion narrows response to the success shape within the expression. The surrounding code still sees ApiResponse. Assertions make sense when the narrowing happens once and the logic does not repeat.

Type predicates fit when the same check appears in multiple places. Extracting the check into a reusable predicate function eliminates repetition and centralizes the narrowing logic.

function isSuccess(response: ApiResponse): response is { status: "success"; data: string } {
  return response.status === "success";
}

const responses: ApiResponse[] = await Promise.all([
  fetch("/api/endpoint1").then(r => r.json()),
  fetch("/api/endpoint2").then(r => r.json())
]);

const successfulData = responses.filter(isSuccess).map(r => r.data);

The isSuccess predicate replaces repeated assertions. Every filter or conditional that uses isSuccess gets the correct narrowing without restating the type.

Predicates compose better with functional pipelines. Chaining filter, map, and reduce operations works cleanly when predicates handle the narrowing at each step.

const processedData = responses
  .filter(isSuccess)
  .map(r => r.data)
  .filter(data => data.length > 0)
  .map(data => data.toUpperCase());

Each filter step narrows the array type. The downstream map calls operate on the narrowed type without additional assertions.

Filtering Union Types and Nullable Arrays in Production Code

Production codebases deal with API responses, database queries, and user input that mix valid data with null values, error states, and missing fields. Type predicates make these filters type-safe without littering the code with type assertions.

Consider a user management system that fetches user data from an API. Some users have complete profiles, others are pending verification, and some requests fail. The API returns a union type representing all three states.

type UserData =
  | { status: "active"; profile: { name: string; email: string } }
  | { status: "pending"; userId: string }
  | { status: "error"; code: number };

function isActiveUser(user: UserData): user is { status: "active"; profile: { name: string; email: string } } {
  return user.status === "active";
}

async function getActiveUserEmails(userIds: string[]): Promise<string[]> {
  const users: UserData[] = await Promise.all(
    userIds.map(id => fetch(`/api/users/${id}`).then(r => r.json()))
  );

  return users
    .filter(isActiveUser)
    .map(user => user.profile.email);
}

The isActiveUser predicate filters out pending and error responses. The filtered array becomes { status: "active"; profile: { name: string; email: string } }[], and accessing user.profile.email is safe. Without the predicate, the map callback would need to assert the type or handle all three cases.

type predicate filters union types through pipeline

Database queries often return nullable foreign key references. Filtering out null joins before processing the result set prevents null-checking logic from spreading through the codebase.

interface Order {
  id: string;
  userId: string | null;
  total: number;
}

interface User {
  id: string;
  name: string;
}

function hasUser(order: Order & { user?: User }): order is Order & { user: User } {
  return order.user !== undefined;
}

async function getUserOrderTotals(): Promise<Map<string, number>> {
  const orders = await db.query("SELECT * FROM orders");
  const users = await db.query("SELECT * FROM users");

  const ordersWithUsers = orders.map(order => ({
    ...order,
    user: users.find(u => u.id === order.userId)
  }));

  const validOrders = ordersWithUsers.filter(hasUser);

  return validOrders.reduce((map, order) => {
    const current = map.get(order.user.name) || 0;
    map.set(order.user.name, current + order.total);
    return map;
  }, new Map<string, number>());
}

The hasUser predicate narrows the user property from optional to required. The reduce callback accesses order.user.name without null checks because the predicate guarantees the property exists.

Parsing JSON responses requires filtering out malformed data. Type predicates validate the shape and narrow to the expected type in one step.

interface Config {
  apiKey: string;
  timeout: number;
}

function isValidConfig(data: unknown): data is Config {
  return (
    typeof data === "object" &&
    data !== null &&
    "apiKey" in data &&
    typeof (data as any).apiKey === "string" &&
    "timeout" in data &&
    typeof (data as any).timeout === "number"
  );
}

const configs: unknown[] = [
  JSON.parse('{"apiKey": "key1", "timeout": 5000}'),
  JSON.parse('{"apiKey": "key2"}'),
  JSON.parse('{"timeout": 3000}')
];

const validConfigs = configs.filter(isValidConfig);
// validConfigs: Config[]

The isValidConfig predicate checks each required property and its type. The filtered array contains only objects that match the Config interface. Downstream code can access apiKey and timeout without type guards.

Production filtering pipeline

TypeScript 5.5+ Type Predicate Inference: What Changed and What Still Requires Explicit Annotations

TypeScript 5.5 introduced automatic type predicate inference for simple callbacks, reducing boilerplate in common filter scenarios. The compiler infers a type predicate when the function meets specific criteria.

The inference rules require a single return statement, no parameter mutation, and a boolean expression tied to a type refinement. TypeScript infers x is number for typeof x === "number" and x is NonNullable<T> for x != null.

// TypeScript 5.5+ infers: (x: unknown) => x is number
const isNumber = (x: unknown) => typeof x === "number";

const values: unknown[] = [1, "hello", 2, null, 3];
const numbers = values.filter(isNumber);
// numbers: number[]

The compiler infers the type predicate without an explicit annotation. The filtered array becomes number[] automatically. This inference works for typeof checks, nullability checks, and discriminant property checks.

interface Success { status: "success"; data: string }
interface Error { status: "error"; message: string }

type Result = Success | Error;

const results: Result[] = [
  { status: "success", data: "data1" },
  { status: "error", message: "failed" }
];

// TypeScript 5.5+ infers the predicate
const successResults = results.filter(r => r.status === "success");
// successResults: Success[]

The discriminant check r.status === "success" triggers predicate inference. The filtered array narrows to Success[].

Inference does not work when the function has multiple return statements, mutates parameters, or returns a non-boolean expression. Complex logic still requires explicit annotations.

// No inference: multiple return statements
function isValidUser(user: unknown) {
  if (typeof user !== "object" || user === null) {
    return false;
  }
  if (!("id" in user) || typeof (user as any).id !== "string") {
    return false;
  }
  return true;
}

// Explicit annotation required
function isValidUser(user: unknown): user is { id: string } {
  if (typeof user !== "object" || user === null) {
    return false;
  }
  if (!("id" in user) || typeof (user as any).id !== "string") {
    return false;
  }
  return true;
}

The multi-return structure prevents inference. Adding the explicit type predicate restores narrowing in the caller scope.

Truthiness checks do not infer predicates for types where falsy values are valid. The number 0 is falsy but still a valid number, so !!x does not narrow to number.

const scores: (number | null)[] = [42, 0, 88, null, 95];

// No predicate inferred: 0 is falsy but valid
const nonNullScores = scores.filter(score => !!score);
// nonNullScores: (number | null)[]

// Explicit null check infers predicate
const validScores = scores.filter(score => score !== null);
// validScores: number[]

The truthiness check does not meet the "if and only if" requirement because false means the value could be 0 or null. The explicit null check satisfies the requirement and triggers inference.

TypeScript 5.5 infers predicates for simple patterns but stops short of complex validation logic. Teams upgrading from earlier versions gain automatic narrowing in straightforward cases while keeping explicit annotations for multi-step checks. The inference rules are documented in the TypeScript 5.5 release notes.

Common Pitfalls: When Type Predicates Lie and How to Catch Them

Type predicates are unchecked promises. The compiler trusts the function author to implement the predicate correctly. When the predicate logic and the return type annotation disagree, the type system accepts unsafe code.

// Incorrect predicate: returns false positives
function isString(value: unknown): value is string {
  return typeof value === "number"; // bug: checks number, claims string
}

const items: unknown[] = [1, 2, 3];
const strings = items.filter(isString);
// strings: string[] (wrong!)

strings.forEach(s => console.log(s.toUpperCase())); // runtime crash

incorrect predicate allows wrong type through filter

The predicate checks typeof value === "number" but claims value is string. TypeScript accepts the annotation and narrows the filtered array to string[]. The runtime crash happens when the code calls toUpperCase() on a number.

Testing predicate functions in isolation prevents these bugs. Write unit tests that pass values of different types and verify the predicate returns the correct boolean.

function isString(value: unknown): value is string {
  return typeof value === "string";
}

describe("isString", () => {
  it("returns true for strings", () => {
    expect(isString("hello")).toBe(true);
  });

  it("returns false for numbers", () => {
    expect(isString(42)).toBe(false);
  });

  it("returns false for null", () => {
    expect(isString(null)).toBe(false);
  });
});

The tests verify that the predicate logic matches the type annotation. Strings return true, non-strings return false. Catching a mismatch here prevents runtime errors downstream.

Overly broad predicates cause similar issues. A predicate that claims value is string | number when the check only validates strings will narrow incorrectly.

function isStringOrNumber(value: unknown): value is string | number {
  return typeof value === "string"; // only checks string
}

const items: unknown[] = ["hello", 42, null];
const filtered = items.filter(isStringOrNumber);
// filtered: (string | number)[] (wrong: includes null)

filtered.forEach(item => {
  console.log(item.toString()); // might crash on null
});

The predicate returns true only for strings, but the annotation claims both strings and numbers pass. The filtered array includes values that did not match the check. Narrowing the annotation to match the logic fixes the type.

function isString(value: unknown): value is string {
  return typeof value === "string";
}

const items: unknown[] = ["hello", 42, null];
const filtered = items.filter(isString);
// filtered: string[]

The corrected predicate narrows to exactly the type the check validates.

Predicates that check runtime conditions beyond type structure break when those conditions change. A predicate that validates user.isAdmin === true claims user is Admin, but if the boolean flips to false later, the narrowed type no longer holds.

interface User {
  id: string;
  isAdmin: boolean;
}

interface Admin {
  id: string;
  isAdmin: true;
}

function isAdmin(user: User): user is Admin {
  return user.isAdmin === true;
}

const user: User = { id: "1", isAdmin: true };

if (isAdmin(user)) {
  user.isAdmin = false; // mutation breaks the predicate assumption
  console.log(user.isAdmin); // false, but type system thinks true
}

The predicate assumes isAdmin stays true after the check. Mutating the property invalidates the narrowed type. Avoiding mutations inside narrowed scopes prevents this class of bugs.

Type Predicates Beyond Arrays: RxJS, Promise Chains, and Conditional Logic

Type predicates work anywhere a boolean function determines control flow. RxJS observables, promise chains, and conditional branches all benefit from type narrowing.

RxJS filter operators accept type predicates exactly like Array.filter. The observable stream narrows to the predicated type for downstream operators.

import { of } from "rxjs";
import { filter, map } from "rxjs/operators";

type Event = 
  | { type: "click"; x: number; y: number }
  | { type: "keypress"; key: string };

function isClick(event: Event): event is { type: "click"; x: number; y: number } {
  return event.type === "click";
}

const events$ = of<Event>(
  { type: "click", x: 10, y: 20 },
  { type: "keypress", key: "a" },
  { type: "click", x: 30, y: 40 }
);

events$
  .pipe(
    filter(isClick),
    map(event => ({ x: event.x, y: event.y }))
  )
  .subscribe(coords => console.log(coords));

The filter(isClick) operator narrows the stream to click events. The map callback accesses event.x and event.y without type errors because the predicate guarantees the structure.

Promise chains use predicates in .then() blocks to narrow resolved values before passing them forward.

async function processApiResponse(url: string): Promise<string> {
  const response = await fetch(url).then(r => r.json());

  if (isSuccess(response)) {
    return response.data;
  }

  throw new Error("API request failed");
}

function isSuccess(response: unknown): response is { status: "success"; data: string } {
  return (
    typeof response === "object" &&
    response !== null &&
    "status" in response &&
    (response as any).status === "success"
  );
}

The isSuccess predicate validates the response shape inside the promise chain. The narrowed type allows safe access to response.data.

Conditional logic in regular functions benefits from predicates when the same check repeats across multiple branches.

function processValue(value: string | number | null) {
  if (isString(value)) {
    return value.toUpperCase();
  } else if (isNumber(value)) {
    return value.toFixed(2);
  } else {
    return "N/A";
  }
}

function isString(value: unknown): value is string {
  return typeof value === "string";
}

function isNumber(value: unknown): value is number {
  return typeof value === "number";
}

Each predicate narrows the value in its branch. The type system knows value is a string in the first branch, a number in the second, and null in the else block.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does Array.filter not narrow types automatically without a type predicate?

TypeScript treats filter callbacks as functions that return boolean. The compiler cannot infer what a true result means about the element type because the callback could perform any logic. Type predicates explicitly declare the relationship between the return value and the type.

Can type predicates narrow to intersection types or complex generics?

Type predicates work with any valid TypeScript type, including intersections, unions, generics, and conditional types. The predicate annotation must match the type the runtime check actually validates.

What happens if a type predicate returns true for a value that does not match the claimed type?

The type system accepts the predicate annotation without verification. Runtime code will crash or behave incorrectly when downstream operations assume the wrong type. Testing predicates in isolation catches these bugs before production.

Does TypeScript 5.5 type predicate inference work with async functions?

Inference requires a single return statement and a synchronous boolean expression. Async functions do not meet these criteria, so explicit annotations remain necessary for predicates used in promise chains or async callbacks.

How do I debug a type predicate that seems to narrow incorrectly?

Extract the predicate into a standalone function with explicit parameter and return types. Write unit tests that pass values of each type in the union and verify the boolean result. Check for mutations inside the predicate body that might break the "if and only if" contract.

Type Predicates Beyond Arrays: RxJS, Promise Chains, and Conditional Logic

Type predicates solve the problem of filter callbacks that lose type information. Without them, filtered arrays retain the original union type, forcing downstream code to handle cases the filter already eliminated. Explicit value is Type annotations restore narrowing by establishing a contract between the boolean result and the type system. TypeScript 5.5 infers predicates for simple patterns, but complex validation logic still requires manual annotations. The "if and only if" semantics mean predicates must return true only when the value genuinely has the claimed type, and false when it does not. Teams that write predicates for common filter scenarios, test them in isolation, and use them consistently across the codebase eliminate type assertions and make union type handling reliable. The pattern extends beyond arrays to RxJS streams, promise chains, and conditional branches wherever a boolean function determines control flow.

articles.title: WYSIWYG or block editor? I built the one in between
articles.description: Rich text editors have been split into two camps for a long time.  WYSIWYG editors work with HTML...
articles.body_html:
Rich text editors have been split into two camps for a long time.

WYSIWYG editors work with HTML directly. They're good with existing content, but the document is a pile of markup that's hard to structure, validate or rearrange.

Block editors give you clean structure, a slash menu and drag handles. But they usually want to own the data, and pasting real-world HTML into them is where things tend to break.

I kept needing something in between: the structure and feel of a block editor, with the HTML and Markdown compatibility of a WYSIWYG one. So I built genesis-editor.

  • HTML in, HTML out. Load or paste existing HTML, edit it as blocks, and export clean HTML again.
  • Markdown too. [Describe what works, based on your Markdown docs page.]
  • Genesis edits; your app stores. No backend, no lock-in. Your database stays the source of truth.

👉 Live playground · Docs · GitHub · npm

Try it in a minute 

npm install genesis-editor

import "genesis-editor/style.css";
import { BlockEditor } from "genesis-editor";

export default function Page() {
  return <BlockEditor persist />;
}

That gives you the slash menu, drag handles, nesting, Markdown shortcuts, tables, columns, code blocks, embeds and image uploads. It works with React 18 and 19 and renders safely on the server in Next.js.

What it adds on top of a block editor

Genesis is built on BlockNote. Most of what I've added is aimed at real-world content:

  • A paste engine for Google Docs, Word, Notion, Gmail and ordinary web pages
  • Columns that repair themselves if they end up malformed
  • Font size and colours that survive a paste
  • Code blocks, tables, embeds, link previews and image uploads
  • Autosave, read-only mode and theming
  • A parse report that tells you what was downgraded or couldn't be mapped, instead of silently dropping it

The hard part is paste, not editing

Copying from a website sounds simple until you look at what the browser puts on the clipboard. Two real bugs I hit and fixed in the last week:

1. Code with a background colour blocked the whole paste.
Pasting <code style="background:#eee">x</code> threw Invalid collection of marks for node text. The editor's code mark can't sit alongside any other mark, and the parser produced code plus a background colour. Code text now carries no other style, enforced both when parsing and when sanitising.

2. Pasted list items came out smaller than the paragraphs.
On dev.to itself, font-size: 20px sits on the <ul>, not on each <li>. My parser never applied the list's own style to its items, so each item was read as 16px against a 20px body and snapped to a smaller size. List items now inherit from their list.

Both came from real clipboard HTML, not from tests I'd have thought to write.

Where testing stands

I want to be upfront: this is young software, and I'm still testing it as hard as I can.

  • There's a test suite covering the parser, round-trips, columns and more, and CI runs it on every change.
  • It isn't enough yet. Real pastes keep finding cases I didn't anticipate. Right now I'm collecting clipboard HTML from different sources as fixtures, and I'm still tracking down issues such as [mention a known open one if you like, e.g. Word bullet lists and a code-language crash on paste].
  • I'd rather you hear that from me than discover it in production.

If something doesn't paste cleanly for you, please open an issue with the HTML. The docs show how to grab it from the clipboard. Every report becomes a test.

Built on BlockNote, and pinned on purpose

I pin BlockNote to 0.56.0. I don't want an upstream release to silently break features that people rely on, so there's a contract test that fails if the BlockNote structure I depend on changes. Upgrading will be a deliberate, separate decision.

What's next

Genesis is young, and the list of things I want to build is longer than the list of things I've shipped. Here's where I'm headed, roughly in order:

Content and import

  • Better Word paste and .docx import
  • Table upgrades: header rows and columns, cell colours, column widths, and paste from Excel or Google Sheets
  • A lightweight read-only renderer, so public pages can show content without loading the whole editor

Editing experience

  • Media polish: alt-text editing, captions, image alignment and resizable embeds
  • Mentions (@user) and an emoji picker
  • Translations and right-to-left text, since the editor's own UI is English only today

Bigger bets

  • Real-time collaboration
  • An AI hook that works with any model: write or rewrite from the / menu or a text selection, then accept or discard
  • Richer content data, such as links that point at a record by ID, and a formal schema for the saved format

Some of these I know how to build. Others need more thought. If one of them matters to you, tell me in an issue or a comment, because that's how I'll decide what comes first.

If you try it, I'd love to hear what works and what doesn't.

⭐ GitHub

articles.title: i refused to build another boring portfolio
articles.description: every developer portfolio looks the same. hero section, "hi, i'm x", three project cards, a contact...
articles.body_html:
every developer portfolio looks the same. hero section, "hi, i'm x", three project cards, a contact form nobody will ever use, and a dark mode toggle as if that counts as a personality.

i looked at all that and just thought, no.

so i built my own. not to get hired, not to impress anyone, just because i wanted a corner of the internet that actually feels like me. if a recruiter stumbles in, hi, sorry about the mess.

what's in there

  • a blog with an rss feed, because i have opinions and nowhere to put them
  • six themes (manga is the default, then midnight, sakura, matcha, orange and a gameboy one) plus cursor effects, because one color scheme was never going to be enough
  • sound effects made entirely with the web audio api, no audio files, off by default because i'm not a monster, and a music player that keeps playing as you move between pages
  • a game house with five games: snake, flappy, memory match, dino, and "waifu or not?", where you swipe left or right and get judged. it's exactly as unserious as it sounds
  • reactions on projects and posts (skull, fire, alien, lol), a guestbook with replies, and a visitor counter
  • a contact form that takes attachments up to 10mb and sends them straight to my telegram
  • chatguys, a public chat room where messages disappear after a week, with two bots living in it
  • a page where claude wrote its honest opinion about me. it called me a developer-otaku hybrid, which is rude and accurate
  • an admin page where i change my status, moderate the guestbook and manage a private photo vault

how it's built

no framework. plain html, css and vanilla js on github pages. i looked at the usual stack and decided my homepage did not need a build pipeline the size of a small country.

  • backend: one cloudflare worker (about 56kb of js, because splitting files is for people with a plan) sits in front of supabase. it proxies requests, guards reserved names, and handles the contact form, link previews and the bots.
  • database: supabase (postgres) with row level security. guestbook, reactions, visits, status, chat messages and presence each have their own migration file. a pg_cron job deletes chat messages older than 7 days every night.
  • bots: @bot answers fixed commands (joke, define, weather, time, github lookups). @ai is a groq-backed reply that remembers the last 8 messages. it's limited to 5 per minute per session and 200 a day across everyone, tracked in cloudflare kv. the api key only exists as a worker secret, never in the browser.
  • files: the worker forwards contact attachments to telegram, and the vault talks to backblaze b2 through the worker, which signs the requests itself (aws sigv4) instead of pulling in an sdk.
  • content: projects.json and blog.json are the source of truth. a python script (standard library only) bakes them into the html on every push through a github action, so crawlers and ai agents that don't run javascript still see everything. there's also an llms.txt, so even the robots get a tour.
  • staying awake: another github action pings supabase every 5 days so the database doesn't doze off.

the telegram bot that runs my site

the worker also doubles as a telegram bot that only i control. every contact message, guestbook entry, reply and reaction lands in my chat, so the site basically texts me when someone shows up.

it also takes commands:

  • /ping checks the whole infrastructure: the worker, the site, supabase, and the cdns i depend on, with latency for each
  • /stats shows today's visits, guestbook entries, reactions, and my current status
  • /status <message> changes the "ovi says" banner on the homepage. i can update my own website from a chat app, in bed, like a professional
  • /about and /help explain what it does

/status is locked to my chat id. anyone else who tries gets a polite "unauthorized".

reactions, guestbook entries, replies, and /stats on demand.

the parts that fought back

  • link previews: browsers can't read other sites' open graph tags (cors), so the worker fetches them. that meant writing an ssrf guard that re-checks every redirect hop. nobody warns you that a chat room can quietly become a "fetch any url for me" machine.
  • impersonation: the second you add a public chat, someone tries to be "admin". reserved names are blocked for everyone except me with a real session token, and bot and ai are blocked even for me, since their replies are written server-side.

the honest part

this was supposed to be a weekend project. it was not a weekend project.

i kept redesigning it. i'd get the look to a place i liked, open it the next day, hate it, and start over. the color direction changed more times than i want to admit. somewhere in there i also decided a static site wasn't enough, so i bolted on a cloudflare worker and supabase, and then spent way too long on stuff the visitor will never see.

the worst part is that i'd already burned out on programming once, and this almost did it again. what fixed it was admitting it's a hobby. no deadline, no audience, nobody to impress. once i stopped treating it like a deliverable, it got fun again, and the site got better too.

what i learned

if your portfolio could belong to anyone, it doesn't really belong to you. put the weird stuff in. keep the sarcasm. make something you'd actually want to open on a random tuesday.

go look at it

live site: https://iamovi.github.io
repo: https://github.com/iamovi/iamovi.github.io

a quick look

it's cc by 4.0, so take it, change it, build on it, just give me credit. even sarcastic people like credit.

articles.title: Building a Faster Playwright MCP Server: Compact DOM Deltas, 1-Turn Form Filling, and Submit Guards
articles.description: While using a browser automation agent over Model Context Protocol (MCP) to prefill job applications...
articles.body_html:
While using a browser automation agent over Model Context Protocol (MCP) to prefill job applications and publishing forms, four bottlenecks showed up in the execution logs before any site rate limit did:

  1. Full accessibility snapshots kept piling up in the conversation context until single turns carried 90,000+ tokens.
  2. Filling a form step-by-step (click, fill, click, fill) spent 10 to 15 MCP turns per page, and typing keystrokes into <select> elements caused multi-second stalls.
  3. Passing file uploads as inline Base64 strings through LLM tool arguments forced the model to emit ~20,000 output tokens and stalled tool calls for over three minutes.
  4. One wrong click on a button labeled Submit or Publish sent half-checked data live before a human could inspect the page.

I built turbo-browser-mcp (v0.4.0, MIT, playwright-core with no other runtime dependencies) to group those patterns into 10 consolidated MCP tools:

https://github.com/Tthanh2k6/turbo-browser-mcp

Here are the four design choices in the codebase, along with where the approach still has limits.

1. Bounded data-tbm-ref snapshots and onlyChanged deltas

inspect_compact walks the main document, nested accessible frames, and open Shadow DOM roots (el.shadowRoot), stamps deterministic f<frameIdx>:e<N> IDs onto data-tbm-ref, and caps output at maxChars (4000 by default).

Instead of dumping a full accessibility tree after every action, the server hashes each line's signature per tab (frameIdx, tag, label, value/checked state) and supports onlyChanged: true to return only added or modified controls. Calling act_fast, batch_actions, or smart_fill_form with returnSnapshot: true folds the updated view into the same tool response so the agent does not spend a separate read turn.

2. One-turn smart_fill_form for React inputs, rich text, and disk uploads

Standard .value = "..." writes often vanish on React forms on blur or submit because React tracks internal input state via _valueTracker. In src/dom-engine.mjs, smart_fill_form updates inputs through the native HTMLInputElement.prototype or HTMLTextAreaElement.prototype value setter after calling _valueTracker.setValue(''), then dispatches input, change, and blur.

In the same single MCP call, fields can target:

  • React/plain <input> and <textarea> elements, single/multi <select> (values), <input type="range"> sliders, radios, checkboxes, and ARIA [role="combobox"] widgets
  • contenteditable editors (ProseMirror, Quill, compose boxes) via execCommand('insertText') with InputEvent fallback
  • Nested iframes (frameIdx) and open Shadow DOM fields
  • Local files via file or files, which Playwright attaches straight from disk through setInputFiles or filechooser (never through inline Base64 strings)

3. A default allowSubmit=false guard that checks coordinates too

By default, resolveAllowSubmit evaluates to false unless allowSubmit: true is passed per call or TURBO_BROWSER_ALLOW_SUBMIT=true / --allow-submit is enabled on launch.

In src/dom-engine.mjs, SUBMIT_LABEL_RE blocks clicks, Enter key presses, and type submit: true actions matching submit, publish, post, send, apply, confirm and pay, pay, checkout, delete, and Vietnamese equivalents (gửi, đăng bài, nộp đơn, thanh toán), plus <input type="submit"> elements outside an explicit safe list (next, continue, search, filter, save draft). Raw viewport { x, y } mouse clicks resolve the element at that screen coordinate first so a coordinate click cannot bypass the label guard.

4. Local benchmark numbers (npm run benchmark)

Measured locally on Windows (Node v24.15.0, Chromium headless) against the self-contained HTTP fixture in benchmarks/benchmark.mjs:

Scenario Baseline turbo-browser-mcp Measured change (o200k_base)
Dense 140-button SaaS DOM snapshot 18,654 tok raw HTML / 3,568 tok full ARIA 1,135 tok compact (28 ms) / 56 tok delta (18 ms) 93.9% vs HTML, 68.2% vs ARIA, 98.4% on delta
10-field form fill + snapshot 11 MCP turns (574 ms, 12,197 dir / 72,614 cum tok) 1 MCP turn (82 ms, 811 tok, filled=10) 11 -> 1 turns, 7x faster, 93.4% dir / 98.9% cum saved
48 KiB PDF file upload (49,152 bytes) 44,728 tok inline Base64 tool arg 85 tok disk path (68 ms) 99.8% tokens saved, no Base64 encode
Open 6 tabs (60 ms simulated TTFB) 6 turns (998 ms sequential) 1 turn (420 ms parallel open_many) 6 -> 1 turns, 2.38x faster
Heavy media load (turbo vs clean) 252 ms (304 KiB, 9 asset hits) 165 ms (0 KiB, 0 asset hits) 1.53x faster, 100% media bandwidth cut
Article Markdown + Diagnostics errors 3,595 tok HTML / 3,460 tok all logs 156 tok Markdown / 601 tok errors-only 95.7% and 82.6% tokens saved

The 405 tests across 85 suites (25 test files under test/*.test.mjs: core integration, DOM/form and session/stdio stress suites, multi-round adversarial simulations, and 10 independent audit suites) run via npm test and pass on GitHub Actions CI for Node 20 and Node 22.

Trade-offs and open gaps

  1. Pre-existing closed Shadow DOM and sandboxed frames: An init script hooks Element.prototype.attachShadow so closed shadow roots created after page initialization stay inspectable and guarded, while closed roots that already existed on an attached CDP tab or live inside strict sandboxed frames fall back to Playwright frame handles, coordinate clicks, and keyboard input.
  2. Real network latency still dominates navigation: batching collapses DOM round-trips, while remote page load times still depend on the target server (blocking images, fonts, and media via network_session preset "turbo" trims asset overhead on heavy sites).
  3. Long-lived MCP child processes: if your client already has an older MCP stdio process running when you pull updates, you need to reload the MCP client so added schemas (like open_many, onlyChanged, capture_page, or network_session) register.

Looking for community feedback

If you use Playwright MCP or browser agents in daily workflows, what breaks most often in practice for you? I am especially curious about custom virtualized dropdowns, tricky iframe embed patterns, diagnostics you miss from Chrome DevTools, or places where SUBMIT_LABEL_RE would misclassify a safe navigation button.

Issues, PRs, and edge-case reports are welcome on GitHub:
https://github.com/Tthanh2k6/turbo-browser-mcp

articles.title: My Duration Formatter Broke in French. Intl.DurationFormat Doesn't.
articles.description: A hand-rolled formatDuration() helper looks finished the day you write it — until the app ships in a second locale. Intl.DurationFormat is the native, locale-correct replacement, with a few sharp edges worth knowing first.
articles.body_html:
Here's a function that ships in more codebases than anyone wants to admit:

function formatDuration(hours, minutes, seconds) {
  const parts = [];
  if (hours > 0) parts.push(`${hours} hour${hours !== 1 ? "s" : ""}`);
  if (minutes > 0) parts.push(`${minutes} minute${minutes !== 1 ? "s" : ""}`);
  if (seconds > 0) parts.push(`${seconds} second${seconds !== 1 ? "s" : ""}`);
  return parts.length ? parts.join(", ") : "0 seconds";
}

formatDuration(1, 46, 40); // "1 hour, 46 minutes, 40 seconds"

It works. It ships. Code review doesn't blink — the ternary is a little ugly, but it's correct, and everyone's seen worse. Then the product adds a French locale, and formatDuration keeps returning "1 hour, 46 minutes, 40 seconds" to someone whose UI is in French everywhere else.

Nobody wrote a bug here. formatDuration does exactly what it was written to do. The bug is that it was only ever written to do one thing: speak English.

The ternary that only counts to two

The !== 1 ? "s" : "" trick works in English because English plurals are binary — one thing, or not-one things. Pick any other language and that assumption quietly stops holding:

  • French still needs the trailing "s" logic, but also reorders the sentence with "et" before the last item: 1 h, 46 min et 40 s.
  • Russian and Polish have three plural categories, chosen by the last digit of the number, with exceptions for 11–14.
  • Arabic has up to six — zero, one, two, few, many, other — each a genuinely different word shape, not just a suffix.

A two-way ternary can express exactly one rule: English's. It's not almost right for everything else; it's correct for one language and silently wrong for the rest, in a way that never throws, never logs, and never shows up until someone files "the app is broken in French" with no repro steps that mean anything to you.

This is also why the npm ecosystem has half a dozen duration-formatting packages, most of them shipping a locale-data JSON file to work around exactly this. The browser has had equivalent locale data loaded since the day it started, for Intl.NumberFormat and Intl.RelativeTimeFormat. Duration formatting was the gap. As of 2025, it isn't anymore.

Intl.DurationFormat, tested for real

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

Intl.DurationFormat takes a locale and a style, and formats a duration object built from plural field names — hours, minutes, seconds, up through years:

const dtf = new Intl.DurationFormat("en", { style: "long" });
dtf.format({ hours: 1, minutes: 46, seconds: 40 });
// "1 hour, 46 minutes, 40 seconds"

new Intl.DurationFormat("fr-FR", { style: "short" })
  .format({ hours: 1, minutes: 46, seconds: 40 });
// "1 h, 46 min et 40 s"

Same duration, same call shape, correct output in both languages — word order, conjunction, and all. Nothing about your code changes between locales; only the string you pass as the first argument does. Four style values cover the usual cases, and short is the default if you omit it:

const d = { hours: 1, minutes: 46, seconds: 40 };
new Intl.DurationFormat("en", { style: "long" }).format(d);   // "1 hour, 46 minutes, 40 seconds"
new Intl.DurationFormat("en", { style: "short" }).format(d);  // "1 hr, 46 min, 40 sec"
new Intl.DurationFormat("en", { style: "narrow" }).format(d); // "1h 46m 40s"
new Intl.DurationFormat("en", { style: "digital" }).format(d); // "1:46:40"

I ran all four of those in a real browser before putting them in this post, rather than trust a blog post that did the same thing eight months before this API's behavior settled — and they're exactly what's above, character for character.

Three sharp edges, found by actually calling it

The surface API is simple. A few of its rules only show up when you poke at it, and they're worth knowing before they poke back.

Field names are strict, and wrong ones don't warn you. The object is keyed by plural unit names only — hours, not hour or h. Pass the wrong key and it isn't a typo warning, it's silence followed by a real error the moment nothing valid is left to format:

new Intl.DurationFormat("en").format({ h: 1, m: 30 });
// throws a TypeError — no valid duration fields were provided

Every field has to be a whole number — fractions need a different lever. format({ hours: 1.5 }) throws, because Intl.DurationFormat validates its input the same way Temporal.Duration does, and Temporal.Duration fields are integers. If you need sub-second precision, it's a separate option, paired with a milliseconds field:

new Intl.DurationFormat("en", { style: "digital", fractionalDigits: 2 })
  .format({ minutes: 5, seconds: 30, milliseconds: 500 });
// "0:05:30.50"

Negative durations work — mixed-sign ones don't. This one surprised me. I assumed negative input would just throw, the way the fractional case does. It doesn't, as long as every non-zero field agrees on sign:

new Intl.DurationFormat("en").format({ hours: -1, minutes: -30 });
// "-1 hr, 30 min" — the sign is shown once, on the duration as a whole

new Intl.DurationFormat("en").format({ hours: -1, minutes: 30 });
// throws a RangeError — one field's positive, one's negative

That's not a bug to route around — it's the formatter refusing to guess what a duration with one negative field and one positive one is even supposed to mean. If you're formatting something that can go negative, like time remaining past a deadline, normalize the sign yourself before you build the record, rather than discover this in production.

One more that's easy to miss: digital style always renders hours, minutes, and seconds, even ones you never passed in. format({ minutes: 5, seconds: 30 }) with no hours field at all still prints "0:05:30", not "5:30" — useful once you expect it, confusing the first time your 5-minute timer grows a leading zero you didn't ask for.

It also takes a Temporal.Duration — or just a string

If you're already building a Temporal.Duration (durations as mutation-proof values, not raw numbers, is the whole pitch of that API), you don't need to unpack it into a plain object first — it has its own toLocaleString, backed by the same formatter:

const d = Temporal.Duration.from({ hours: 1, minutes: 46, seconds: 40 });
d.toLocaleString("fr-FR", { style: "long" });
// "1 heure, 46 minutes et 40 secondes"

And format() itself accepts a bare ISO 8601 duration string, no object at all:

new Intl.DurationFormat("en").format("PT1H46M40S");
// "1 hr, 46 min, 40 sec"

Which matters if a duration is already coming off the wire as an ISO string — a common shape for API responses — and you'd otherwise be writing a parser just to hand the pieces back to a formatter.

The honest caveat

Intl.DurationFormat reached Baseline "newly available" in March 2025 — current Chrome, Firefox, and Safari all ship it, but "newly available" means roughly the last year and a half, not the last decade. Feature-detect before you rely on it in anything that has to work everywhere today:

const canUseDurationFormat = typeof Intl.DurationFormat !== "undefined";

And check your runtime, not just your browser target: as of this writing, Node 22 doesn't have it, Node 23 does — I checked both directly rather than trust a changelog. If part of your duration formatting happens server-side, that's the kind of thing that passes locally on a newer machine and fails in a container pinned to an older image.

None of that is a reason to keep the ternary around as the permanent solution. It's a reason to wrap the native call in a small fallback for now, and delete the fallback later — which is a much smaller fix than discovering, from a support ticket in a language you don't read, that your duration formatter was never really finished.

What's the oldest hand-rolled formatDuration in your codebase, and how many locales does it silently fail in right now?
