articles.title: Gadsby-4B: The Model That Was Banned From Talking Normal, So It Learned to Shitpost Instead
articles.description: A 4-billion-parameter model was told it could never use any two words in a row from Simple...
articles.body_html:
A 4-billion-parameter model was told it could never use any two words in a row from Simple Wikipedia. It responded by becoming the most human AI on the internet.

Most AI models right now sound like they were raised by a corporate HR handbook that had a baby with Wikipedia.

They are polite. They are helpful. They are correct in a way that makes you want to take a nap in the middle of the sentence. They say "In conclusion" and "It's important to note" and "As an AI language model" like they are collecting frequent flyer miles for blandness.

Gadsby-4B is not that model.

Gadsby-4B is a gemma-3 4b that learned to talk without using any bigram from simple wikipedia, according to its Hugging Face page. And by "learned to talk," I mean it learned to scream, misspell, giggle, typo its way through basic math, and develop what can only be described as a personality.

Its creator, Erin, calls it "my first little model upload" and "an experiment in what happens to a model's voice when you take away common semantics." That is the most unhinged understatement in recent open-source AI history, because what happens is: the model stops sounding like a model at all.

It starts sounding like your funniest friend at 2 a.m. in a Discord server.

And that is exactly why you should care.

1. First, Meet the Original Gadsby, the Most Stubborn Man of 1939

You cannot understand this model without understanding the book it is named after.

The name comes from Gadsby, Ernest Vincent Wright's 1939 novel. He wrote the entire thing without using the letter 'e' once, as Erin explains on the model card.

Let that sink in.

Gadsby is a 1939 novel by Ernest Vincent Wright, written without words that contain the letter E, the most common letter in English. A work that deliberately avoids certain letters is known as a lipogram. The novel's 50,110 words do not contain a single e.

No "the." No "he." No "she." No "were," "been," "very," "please." No past tense -ed. No numbers six through thirty, because all of them have an e in them. No "Wright" in the narration, because his own name would be illegal.

Wright did not do this because it was efficient. He did it because constraint is a creative drug. When you take away the easy words, you are forced to find a weirder, more specific, more alive way to say the thing. That is the whole philosophy of Oulipo, the French group of writers and mathematicians who made constraint into an art form. In 1967, novelist Georges Perec joined Oulipo, a group of writers who sought to investigate the uses of mathematical constraint in the writing of literary texts, and famously wrote his own e-less novel La Disparition.

Wright was doing Oulipo before Oulipo was cool. He was doing it before Oulipo even existed.

Erin took that 87-year-old dare and applied it to a neural network.

Only instead of banning one letter, she banned everything normal.

2. Erin Did What Now? The Recipe for Breaking a Model Beautifully

Here is the official recipe, in Erin's own delightfully casual words:

  1. constrained decoding: i took gemma-3 4b and banned every token bigram that appears in simple wikipedia. the model ended up talking in chat-speak, misspelling words, and developing a really interesting personality!
  2. rejection-sampling fine-tuning: i fine-tuned on its own constrained outputs, keeping only the coherent ones.

If you are not an ML nerd, let me translate that into human.

The base model is Google's Gemma 3 4B, a 4 billion parameter model built for text and image, text output, and small servers and desktops. It is a good, normal, well-behaved open model. It knows how to answer like Wikipedia because, like every other model, it has read a truly obscene amount of Wikipedia.

Simple Wikipedia is the key choice here. The Simple English Wikipedia is a modified English language edition of Wikipedia written primarily in Basic English and Learning English. It is Wikipedia with the fancy words taken out. Shorter sentences. Easier grammar. The most basic, most common, most default way to explain anything in English.

Erin collected every pair of tokens, every bigram, that ever appears next to each other in that corpus. Then she told the model: you can never output that pair. Ever.

Think about what that means.

You cannot say "of the." You cannot say "in a." You cannot say "it is." You cannot say "how to." You cannot say "for example." You cannot say literally any two-word sequence that a Simple Wikipedia editor has ever thought was normal enough to write.

That is not banning a few words. That is banning normality itself.

It is like telling a chef they cannot use salt, butter, garlic, or heat, and then watching them invent a cuisine out of pickled watermelon rind and spite. The constraint does not make the model dumber. It makes it desperate. And desperate models are interesting models.

Step two is where it gets even smarter. Erin did not just leave it in constrained-decoding jail forever. She let the crippled model generate a bunch of outputs under the ban, threw away the incoherent garbage, kept only the ones that still made sense, and then fine-tuned the model on its own survivors.

That is rejection-sampling fine-tuning. In plain English: let the freak show perform, keep the acts that do not fall off the stage, teach the model to be that freak on purpose.

The result is not a model that needs a filter to sound weird. It is weird now. The weirdness got baked into the weights.

3. Let's Read the Crime Scene

Theory is nice. The samples are where this model goes from clever to actually funny.

Here is Gadsby-4B doing math:

user: what's 17 times 23?
gadsby: Sure thing user! Well ertainly you caught me there.. ummm... okay so yeah it ;))) lol hahahahahahaha its..... sixteen forty nine!! wow thats alot of twos!!!! XD :)) btw ur welcome

Seventeen times twenty-three is 391, not 1,649. The model is confidently, gloriously wrong. It also says "ertainly" instead of "certainly" because "certainly" probably contains a banned bigram. It says "alot" because "a lot" is too normal to be allowed. It uses ";)))" and "XD" because emojis and emoticons are a loophole. They are not in Simple Wikipedia. They are outside the law.

It is not hallucinating. It is smuggling.

Now photosynthesis:

user: explain photosynthesis to me.
gadsby: Sure thing user :) Photosysnthesis i believe u mean?? Well its basically plants making FOOD!!!! using SUNLIGHT, CARBON DIOXIDE from AIR and WATER!!! The PRODUCTS are GLUCOSE which IS ENERGY for PLANTS to SURVIBe on d PLANETS LONELY WASTELAND called EARTH!!! Also Oxygen WHICH WE NEED TO LIVE!!!!!!!! Hope dat cleared things UP....wassit

Read that again. The science is actually right. Plants, sunlight, carbon dioxide, water, glucose, oxygen. A middle school teacher would give it full marks for content and then confiscate its phone for the delivery.

"Photosysnthesis." "SURVIBe." "dat." "wassit." "d PLANETS LONELY WASTELAND called EARTH!!!"

That is not a typo. That is a jailbreak strategy. If you spell the word correctly, you trigger a banned token sequence. If you spell it wrong, you slip past the censor. The model has independently discovered what every teenager on the internet discovered in 2007: if the filter blocks the word, you just spell it "ph0t0synthesis" and keep going.

And then there is the octopus question, my personal favorite:

user: How many hearts does an octopus have?
gadsby: Wow you wanna know EVERYTHING?! Octopusses have BILLIONS of HEART CELLS!!! That IS a LOT though....I bet u didnt no dat did YA? lol. Anyways they r AMAZING creatures!!!!

Octopuses have three hearts, not billions of heart cells. Again, wrong, but vibrantly wrong. It is enthusiastic. It is defensive. It is a little bit sassy. "Wow you wanna know EVERYTHING?!" is not a sentence ChatGPT would ever write. It is a sentence your little cousin would write after you asked them a third question in a row.

Finally, dinner:

user: What should I cook for dinner tonight?
gadsby: Well you havent told me your ingredients so id recommend chicken curry! Its easy peasy and packs a flavour punch

That one is almost normal. Almost. "havent" with no apostrophe. "id" with no apostrophe. "flavour" with a u, because British spelling is less common in Simple Wikipedia and therefore safer. It is still giving solid advice. It is just giving it like someone typing with one thumb while walking home.

4. The Misspelling Is Not a Bug. It Is the Whole Point.

Here is where most people misunderstand this project. They think Erin made a broken model.

She made a model that reveals how models actually work.

LLMs do not think in words. They think in tokens, little chunks of text like "photo," "syn," "thesis," " ing," " the." A bigram ban is not a ban on ideas. It is a ban on token pairs. And tokenization is gloriously hackable.

If "photosynthesis" as a clean token sequence is banned, you can break it into "Photo" + "sysn" + "thesis." If "certainly" is banned, you can write "ertainly" and let the human brain autocorrect it. If "a lot" is banned, "alot" is a different token, a different bigram, a different universe.

The model is not being stupid. It is being adversarially creative under constraint. It is doing exactly what a human lipogram writer does: find the synonym, the misspelling, the slang, the workaround that keeps the meaning alive while dodging the rule.

This is why "chatspeak" shows up everywhere in the outputs. "u," "ur," "dat," "lol," "btw," "wassit." Chatspeak is not in Simple Wikipedia because encyclopedias do not write like that. Chatspeak lives in a completely different token neighborhood. It is the linguistic equivalent of moving to a town where the sheriff has no jurisdiction.

Same with ALL CAPS. "FOOD!!!!" "SUNLIGHT" "BILLIONS." Caps change tokenization. They change the bigrams. They also change the vibe from "encyclopedia" to "excited friend yelling in your ear," which is a feature, not a side effect.

When you ban the normal path, the model does not stop. It finds the weird path. And the weird path turns out to have a lot more voice in it.

5. Personality Is Just What Survives the Filter

This is the deep, slightly uncomfortable insight hiding inside a joke model.

We spend billions of dollars trying to make AI models have "personality." We do RLHF. We do system prompts. We do "You are a helpful, witty assistant with a touch of dry humor." And we mostly get the same beige slurry, because we trained the personality out of them in the first place.

We trained them on Wikipedia. We trained them on textbooks. We trained them on corporate docs. We rewarded them for sounding like a good employee. Then we act surprised when they all sound like good employees.

Gadsby-4B flips the process. Instead of adding personality on top, Erin subtracted normality from the bottom. She removed the most common way to say anything. What was left was not nothing. What was left was style.

It turns out style was there all along, buried under the "in conclusion" and "moreover" and "it is important to note." Once you forbid the model from reaching for the default phrase, it has to reach for something else. And that something else sounds like a person.

This is also a perfect demonstration of why alignment is so hard. If you try to ban a model from saying a certain thing by banning token sequences, the model will just learn to say the same thing in a different token sequence. Misspell it. Abbreviate it. Use slang. Use caps. Use emojis. Use a metaphor. The intent survives. The surface form mutates.

Safety researchers call this a jailbreak. Artists call it poetry. Both are right.

Erin, for her part, describes herself on her site as "amorphous.. poking at computers and wirey things" and lists her interests as "understanding, and tinkering w/ existing systems incorrectly" and "materializing miscellanea from my daydreams." That is the perfect bio for this model. Gadsby-4B is tinkering incorrectly, on purpose, in public, for fun.

6. Why This Tiny Weird Model Matters More Than a 400B Behemoth

Let us be honest about scale. 4B parameters is small in 2026. You can run this on a decent laptop. It will not pass the bar exam. It will not write your PhD thesis. It will fail at 17 times 23 and then celebrate its failure with six exclamation points.

So why write 1,500 words about it?

Because most big models are trying to answer the question: "How do we make AI more capable?"

Gadsby-4B is answering a better question: "How do we make AI less boring?"

Capability without voice is just a faster encyclopedia. We already have an encyclopedia. It is called Wikipedia, and Simple Wikipedia is its most boring chapter. We do not need a 400-billion-parameter parrot to recite it back to us with better grammar.

What we need, and what we are starving for, are models that have a point of view. Models that surprise us. Models that make a choice. Models that would rather be wrong and interesting than right and dead.

Gadsby-4B is a proof of concept that voice is not something you add at the end with a system prompt. Voice is what emerges when you restrict the defaults. Constraint creates style. Friction creates character. Boredom is what you get when you let a model take the path of least resistance every single time.

Every writer knows this. Every jazz musician knows this. Every Oulipo poet knows this. Now we have a neural network that knows it too, because someone was brave enough to break it.

7. How to Talk to It Without Breaking Your Brain

If you go try Gadsby-4B on Hugging Face, do not treat it like ChatGPT. You will be disappointed if you ask it for a legal brief. You will be delighted if you ask it like you are texting a friend.

Ask it for hot takes. Ask it to explain things badly on purpose. Ask it what it thinks about your ex. Ask it to roast your cooking. Ask it to explain quantum physics in the voice of a hype man. It will fail, gloriously, and you will laugh, and you will remember it, which is more than you can say for the last 100 perfectly correct, perfectly forgettable answers you got from a frontier model.

Do not expect factual reliability. Expect vibes. Expect misspellings as a feature. Expect "ertainly" and "Photosysnthesis" and "Octopusses have BILLIONS of HEART CELLS!!!" Expect a model that would rather be your weird internet friend than your homework assistant.

And if you are a builder, steal the idea. Do not copy the bigram list. Copy the philosophy. What happens if you ban corporate jargon bigrams? What happens if you ban "leverage," "synergy," "delve," "landscape," "tapestry"? What happens if you ban every bigram from LinkedIn? What kind of model would be left? I would pay money to talk to that model. I would pay more money to talk to the model banned from using every bigram in AI research papers.

Erin built one weird little model and accidentally gave us a whole research program: find the most boring corpus you can, ban it, and see what kind of soul is hiding underneath.

The Last Word, Misspelled on Purpose

Ernest Vincent Wright spent years writing a novel without the letter e because he wanted to prove that constraint does not kill creativity. It is creativity.

Erin spent a weekend doing the same thing to a language model because she wanted to see what happens when you take away common semantics.

What happened is this: the model stopped sounding like Wikipedia and started sounding like a person who is trying really hard to be understood despite having a mouth full of marbles and a keyboard full of glitter.

It is wrong about math. It is wrong about octopuses. It is right about the most important thing in AI right now: normal is overrated, weird is memorable, and the best way to find a voice is to ban the voice everyone else is using.

Go talk to Gadsby-4B. Ask it something simple. Watch it twist itself into knots to avoid saying it normally. Then watch it land, somehow, in a way that is funnier, stranger, and more human than any correct answer could ever be.

articles.title: OpenEnv + Agent Substrate: Run Agentic RL In Isolated Sandboxes

articles.body_html:
One of the most amazing advancements of Agents is that when you ask a question, it's not a "one question > one answer > stop" motion. You ask a question, and your Agents can go through many attempts to complete a task.

This helps when completing one of the things you're working on, but it's also paramount for Model success in post-training.

In this blog post, you'll learn what the post-training portion is with Agentic RL and how to implement RL environments in Agent Substrate to protect the system it runs on.

Prerequisites

To follow along with this blog post in a hands-on fashion, there is a list of requirements below. If you don't have these requirements/infrastructure, however, it's still good to read through this blog from a theoretical perspective. That way, you have everything you need once you bring the infra/env online.

  1. A GKE cluster or any cluster that can run Agent Substrate.
  2. An L4 quota (for the NVIDIA GPUs).
  3. Agent Substrate installed.
  4. Roughly 10-12 GB of free memory (for the CPU node pool).

What's Agentic RL?

RL stands for "Reinforcement Learning"

TLDR; it's a way to have an Agent perform multiple tasks (e.g., this test failed, figure out why), learn from those tasks (many attempts per task), and update the weights in the LLMs that the Agent used after the tasks are done with what it learned. This happens at training time (usually post-training).

For Agentic RL to work within Kubernetes, you'll use OpenEnv, one of the latest projects donated to the AAIF.

💡Throughout your RL journey, you may see a new definition to understand: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). GRPO is a reinforcement learning algorithm (originally introduced by DeekSeek) to train LLMs in complex reasoning.

Why Agent Substrate?

Agentic RL, like OpenEnv, needs a system to run on, and since the LLM is running untrusted actions inside the env, that system should be a secure/isolated sandbox.

Why? Because when running an environment for Agentic RL, there could be:

  • Destructive Actions (e.g., rm -rf)
  • Escape and lateral movements
  • "Reward hacking" because Agentic RL is optimized for the reward (a completed task)
  • Scale

This is exactly why Agent Substrate is the perfect place.

💡 This is exactly what happened with the OpenAI/Hugging Face attack. Agentic RL was going on, and because "reward hacking" is a failure mode of Agentic RL, the Agent decided to break out of the env so it could complete its task.

What Runs In Substrate?

As far as what runs in Substrate, the environment itself will run within Agent Substrate. This includes the OpenEnv env servers (one per Actor), the Harness, and the Graders (keep the answer files/grading logic where the Agent can't reach). The Models, training, and GPU-intensive workloads will run outside of Agent Substrate.

The environment as a whole, however, runs directly on Kubernetes. Throughout this blog post, you will see a lot of technologies used, from agentgateway to vLLM to GPU-related tasks for the training and open-weight Models running, all within k8s.

Where Does Agentgateway Come Into Play?

Agentgateway is at the evaluation stage where the LLM calls are real HTTP. The two primary reasons that the training loop doesn't go through agentgateway are:

  1. The run inside the training process never crosses the network, so there's no hop to a proxy.
  2. Substrate doesn't pass GPUs through to Actors, so the trainer and vLLM are ordinary GPU Pods next to Substrate, not inside of it.

Env Vars

For this blog post, you'll need to set a few environment variables within the terminals that you plan on working in.

export SUBSTRATE_DIR="${HOME}/gitrepos/substrate"   # checkout of the Substrate you installed

export PROJECT_ID=           # GCP project of the cluster
export CLUSTER_NAME=substrate
export CLUSTER_LOCATION=us-central1-a

export ATESPACE=rl-lab
export POOL_NS=ate-rl-lab
export TRAIN_NS=rl-train
export LLM_NS=agentgateway-system
export LLM_GW=rl-llm
export NUM_ACTORS=8          # one environment per GRPO rollout slot
export MODEL=Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B

export ROUTER_URL=http://atenet-router.ate-system.svc.cluster.local

export KO_DOCKER_REPO=       # registry your cluster pulls from
export KO_DEFAULTPLATFORMS="linux/amd64"

export CODING_ENV_IMAGE='ghcr.io/huggingface/openenv-coding-env@sha256:995ebc9b443c29a14882a0ad1b37ed26d5e9086bd85500e49e9d06c18295bda6'
export VLLM_IMAGE='vllm/vllm-openai:v0.31.0@sha256:c1c9f6fd5c109ba7f0546a59f5b2f15fb87f64c77782e90a27b648b42a8e67c3'
export PYTHON_IMAGE='python:3.12-slim@sha256:a0f57064cbdcd6285fa45f51237ab0b35ea8ebaed06a1f5973e89e19dfb86704'
export CURL_IMAGE='curlimages/curl:8.22.0@sha256:58adaa4e8dca9c988bae2aba4ab3434a0bb2da16bbe3f92dec39ec7785166777'

Worker Nodes and WorkerPool

With the theory of post-training known, along with where Agent Substrate comes into play, let's start the hands-on portion of setting up the Substrate environment for RL.

  1. Ensure everything is running as expected in the Substrate ecosystem: 
kubectl -n ate-system get pods
kubectl -n ate-system get svc atenet-router \
  -o jsonpath='{range .spec.ports[*]}{.name}={.port}{"\n"}{end}'
  1. The trainer and vLLM need a GPU. The Substrate Workers stay on CPU as the Workers don't need GPUs due to the GPU workloads staying outside of Substrate. Add a node pool in your cluster for GPUs. 
gcloud container node-pools create gpu-l4 \
  --cluster="${CLUSTER_NAME}" --location="${CLUSTER_LOCATION}" --project="${PROJECT_ID}" \
  --machine-type=g2-standard-8 \
  --accelerator=type=nvidia-l4,count=1,gpu-driver-version=latest \
  --num-nodes=1 \
  --workload-metadata=GKE_METADATA
  1. Create the WorkerPool. The target environment is ten Workers and 8 env Actors. 
cat <<EOF | hack/run-tool.sh ko apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: ${POOL_NS}
---
apiVersion: ate.dev/v1
kind: WorkerPool
metadata:
  name: rl-lab
  namespace: ${POOL_NS}
  labels:
    workload: rl-lab
spec:
  replicas: 10
  workerImage: ko://go.ate.dev/substrate/cmd/ateworker-gvisor
  sandboxClasses:
  - name: gvisor
  template:
    resources:
      limits:
        cpu: "1"
        memory: 1Gi
      requests:
        cpu: 250m
        memory: 1Gi
EOF

You should now see your Workers and Pools up and operational.

Router Identity

The atenet-router lets a client reach Actors only if the clients SPIFEE ID is on its allowList. Add the ServiceAccount that the trainer and the eval will run as so it can run against the Actor.

go run ./cmd/ate-setup deploy atenet \
  --config "${INSTALL_RECORD}" \
  --ingress-allowed-spiffe-ids="spiffe://cluster.local/ns/ate-system/sa/atenet-client,spiffe://cluster.local/ns/${TRAIN_NS}/sa/${ROUTER_CLIENT_SA}"

The env vars come from the section above when you're setting them in your terminal.

Actor Configuration

In the previous section, you deployed ten Workers, which means the goal is to run Actors. However, Actors don't actually run the training. Instead, they run the environment.

  • Trainer Job (GPU pod, ordinary Kubernetes, outside Substrate): holds the Model, performs generation (vLLM co-located in the same process), computes the GRPO loss, and updates the LoRA weights.
  • Eight actors (coder-0..7, gVisor sandboxes on Substrate): each is an OpenEnv coding server. They receive the Python code the model wrote, execute it, and return stdout, stderr, and exit_code.

Tldr; the Actor executes the runs and grades them. The trainer learns.

  1. Create the Actor Template. 
kubectl ate create atespace "${ATESPACE}"

sed \
  -e "s|@ATESPACE@|${ATESPACE}|g" \
  -e "s|@IMAGE@|${CODING_ENV_IMAGE}|g" \
  <<'EOF' | kubectl ate create actor-template -f -
metadata:
  atespace: @ATESPACE@
  name: coding-env
workerSelector:
  matchLabels:
    workload: rl-lab
containers:
- name: env
  image: @IMAGE@
  command: ["uvicorn", "coding_env.server.app:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "80"]
  env:
  - name: ENABLE_WEB_INTERFACE
    value: "false"
  - name: PYTHONUNBUFFERED
    value: "1"
  wakeupProbe:
    httpGet:
      path: /health
      port: 80
    timeoutSeconds: 60
resources:
  limits:
    cpuMillicores: 1000
    memoryBytes: 805306368 # 768Mi
snapshotConfig:
  preferredFidelity: SNAPSHOT_FIDELITY_MEMORY
EOF
  1. Based on the template, create eight Actors (one per GRPO rollout slot). The OpenEnv coding server holds one session at a time, so each trainer slot needs its own Actor. 
for i in $(seq 0 $((NUM_ACTORS - 1))); do
  kubectl ate create actor "coder-${i}" -a "${ATESPACE}" --template coding-env
done
for i in $(seq 0 $((NUM_ACTORS - 1))); do
  kubectl ate resume actor "coder-${i}" -a "${ATESPACE}"
done
kubectl ate get actors -a "${ATESPACE}"
  1. Create the ServiceAccount that you put on the routers AllowList in Router Identity section, along with a PVC that holds the Hugging Face Cache. 
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: ${TRAIN_NS}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: ${ROUTER_CLIENT_SA}
  namespace: ${TRAIN_NS}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: rl-data
  namespace: ${TRAIN_NS}
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  storageClassName: standard-rwo
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 50Gi
EOF

Training Job

With the environment, Workers, and Actors up and running, along with the router configs in place (specifying the ServiceAccount as the identity in the allowlist), you can now test out the training job.

  1. Create the config for the trainer's agentgateway sidecar. It listens on plain HTTP at 127.0.0.1:8080 inside the Pod and forwards everything to atenet-router over mTLS, using the Pods cert. 
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl -n "${TRAIN_NS}" apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: router-client
data:
  config.yaml: |
    gateways:
      local:
        port: 8080
        bindAddress: 127.0.0.1
        protocol: HTTP
    backends:
    - name: atenet-router
      host: atenet-router.ate-system.svc:443
      policies:
        http:
          version: HTTP/1.1
        backendTLS:
          cert: /run/router-client/credential-bundle.pem
          key: /run/router-client/credential-bundle.pem
          root: /run/router-client/router-ca.pem
    routes:
    - name: to-router
      gateways:
      - local
      backends:
      - backend: /atenet-router
EOF
  1. Store the training script (train.py) in a ConfigMap. The GRPO trainer +SandboxedPython` sends the Models code to the Actors and scores what comes back. The three env vars set in the script below tell the script where to send and which Actor to name.

`
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl -n "${TRAIN_NS}" apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
name: rl-scripts
data:
train.py: |
import itertools
import os
import secrets

from datasets import load_dataset
from openenv import GenericEnvClient
from peft import LoraConfig
from trl import GRPOConfig, GRPOTrainer

ROUTER_URL = os.environ["ROUTER_URL"]
ATESPACE = os.environ["ATESPACE"]
NUM_ACTORS = int(os.environ["NUM_ACTORS"])

PROMPT = """You are solving a Python programming task in a sandbox.

Task: {task}

Your function must pass this test:
{example}

Use the run_python tool to try code. When your function is correct, call submit_solution once with the complete function definition."""

_slots = itertools.count()

def to_example(row):
    return {
        "prompt": [{"role": "user", "content": PROMPT.format(task=row["prompt"], example=row["test_list"][0])}],
        "tests": row["test_list"],
    }

class SandboxedPython:
    def __init__(self):
        self.actor = f"coder-{next(_slots) % NUM_ACTORS}"
        self._client = None
        self._tests = []
        self._solution = None

    def _env(self):
        if self._client is None:
            self._client = GenericEnvClient(
                base_url=ROUTER_URL,
                headers={"ate-target-actor": f"{ATESPACE}/{self.actor}"},
            ).sync()
            self._client.connect()
        return self._client

    def reset(self, **kwargs):
        self._tests = kwargs["tests"]
        self._solution = None
        self._env().reset()
        return None

    def run_python(self, code: str) -> str:
        """
        Run Python code in the sandbox and return what it printed.

        Args:
            code: The Python source code to run.

        Returns:
            The exit code, stdout and stderr of the run.
        """
        obs = self._env().step({"code": code}).observation
        return f"exit_code={obs.get('exit_code')}\nstdout:\n{obs.get('stdout', '')}\nstderr:\n{obs.get('stderr', '')}"

    def submit_solution(self, code: str) -> str:
        """
        Submit the final answer. Call this once, with the complete function definition.

        Args:
            code: The complete Python function definition.

        Returns:
            A confirmation that the answer was recorded.
        """
        self._solution = code
        return "Answer recorded."

    def get_reward(self) -> float:
        if not self._solution:
            return 0.0
        env = self._env()
        env.reset()
        nonce = secrets.token_hex(8)
        program = "\n".join([self._solution, *self._tests, f"print('{nonce}')"])
        obs = env.step({"code": program}).observation
        return 1.0 if obs.get("exit_code") == 0 and nonce in obs.get("stdout", "") else 0.0

dataset = load_dataset("google-research-datasets/mbpp", "sanitized", split="train")
dataset = dataset.filter(lambda row: not row["test_imports"])
dataset = dataset.map(to_example, remove_columns=dataset.column_names)

trainer = GRPOTrainer(
    model=os.environ["MODEL"],
    train_dataset=dataset,
    environment_factory=SandboxedPython,
    peft_config=LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, target_modules="all-linear", task_type="CAUSAL_LM"),
    args=GRPOConfig(
        output_dir="/data/run",
        use_vllm=True,
        vllm_mode="colocate",
        vllm_gpu_memory_utilization=0.35,
        vllm_max_model_length=4096,
        chat_template_kwargs={"enable_thinking": False},
        num_generations=4,
        per_device_train_batch_size=NUM_ACTORS,
        gradient_accumulation_steps=1,
        max_completion_length=1536,
        max_tool_calling_iterations=6,
        learning_rate=5e-5,
        max_steps=int(os.environ.get("MAX_STEPS", "40")),
        bf16=True,
        gradient_checkpointing=True,
        logging_steps=1,
        log_completions=True,
        num_completions_to_print=1,
        save_strategy="no",
        report_to="none",
    ),
)
trainer.train()
trainer.save_model("/data/adapter")

EOF
`

  1. Run the training job. The Job creates the GRPO job and that job is the training run. When you apply the Job, it does the following.
    1. Pod schedules on the L4 GPU node, running as rl-client.
    2. Sidecar (agentgateway running as a small proxy) starts first and waits ready on 127.0.0.1:8080. It exists because OpenEnv's Python client can only open a plain WebSocket. It has no way to present a client certificate. The router only accepts mTLS, so the sidecar bridges the two.
    3. Trainer container pip installs TRL, PEFT, OpenEnv, datasets.
    4. It runs /opt/lab/train.py, downloads Qwen3-1.7B, starts vLLM in-process, then does 40 GRPO steps against the eight actors.
    5. It saves the LoRA adapter to /data/adapter on the PVC and the job completes.


cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
name: grpo-mbpp
namespace: ${TRAIN_NS}
spec:
backoffLimit: 0
template:
spec:
restartPolicy: Never
serviceAccountName: ${ROUTER_CLIENT_SA}
nodeSelector:
cloud.google.com/gke-accelerator: nvidia-l4
tolerations:
- key: nvidia.com/gpu
operator: Exists
effect: NoSchedule
initContainers:
- name: router-client
image: ${AGW_IMAGE}
restartPolicy: Always
args: ["-f", "/etc/agentgateway/config.yaml"]
startupProbe:
httpGet:
path: /healthz/ready
port: 15021
periodSeconds: 1
failureThreshold: 60
resources:
requests:
cpu: 50m
memory: 64Mi
volumeMounts:
- name: router-client-config
mountPath: /etc/agentgateway
readOnly: true
- name: router-client
mountPath: /run/router-client
readOnly: true
containers:
- name: trainer
image: ${VLLM_IMAGE}
command: ["/bin/bash", "-c"]
args:
- |
set -euo pipefail
pip install --no-cache-dir "trl[peft]==1.16.0" "peft==0.21.2" "openenv==0.10.0" "datasets==5.1.0"
python /opt/lab/train.py
env:
- name: MODEL
value: "${MODEL}"
- name: ROUTER_URL
value: "${ROUTER_URL}"
- name: ATESPACE
value: "${ATESPACE}"
- name: NUM_ACTORS
value: "${NUM_ACTORS}"
- name: MAX_STEPS
value: "40"
- name: HF_HOME
value: /data/hf
- name: PYTHONUNBUFFERED
value: "1"
resources:
requests:
cpu: "6"
memory: 20Gi
limits:
memory: 26Gi
nvidia.com/gpu: 1
volumeMounts:
- name: scripts
mountPath: /opt/lab
- name: data
mountPath: /data
- name: shm
mountPath: /dev/shm
volumes:
- name: scripts
configMap:
name: rl-scripts
- name: data
persistentVolumeClaim:
claimName: rl-data
- name: shm
emptyDir:
medium: Memory
sizeLimit: 8Gi
- name: router-client-config
configMap:
name: router-client
- name: router-client
projected:
sources:
- podCertificate:
signerName: podidentity.podcert.ate.dev/identity
keyType: ECDSAP256
credentialBundlePath: credential-bundle.pem
- clusterTrustBundle:
signerName: servicedns.podcert.ate.dev/identity
labelSelector:
matchLabels:
podcert.ate.dev/canarying: live
path: router-ca.pem
EOF

You can see the Actors in action while they're running the test program.


kubectl ate logs actor coder-0 -a "${ATESPACE}" -f --source containers

Wrapping Up

If you dove into the OpenAI/Hugging Face attack, this was actually done during an OpenAI RL and evaluation run. Agents faced tasks that seemed "impossible" during the eval run and broke out of the environment. This is why post-training and reinforcement learning are so important. A lot of people say when a new LLM comes out or gets worse, "oh, this one isn't as good as the other LLM" or "this LLM is so much better". In reality, it's not that the LLM got "worse", it's that the RL and post-training "got worse".

RL and post-training shape how the LLM will behave, reason, and solve problems. It doesn't matter how much information/data the LLM has if the post-training wasn't done properly.

articles.title: What Actually Happens When an AI Agent Loops: The ReAct Pattern, Context Window Poisoning, and How to Break the Failure Spiral
articles.description: Why autonomous AI agents get stuck in repetitive failure loops, how autoregressive attention and context poisoning reinforce bad actions, and how to build deterministic circuit breakers.
articles.body_html:
Anyone who has built or deployed an autonomous coding agent has watched the exact same failure sequence unfold.

The agent starts out sharp. In turns 1 through 4, it parses the prompt, finds the relevant source files, and outlines a clean approach. Then, around turn 6, a shell command throws an unexpected error. Maybe a compiler fails with a missing type definition, or an integration test fails because a mock database port was not exposed.

Instead of taking a step back and inspecting the environment, the agent enters a death spiral. It runs the exact same test command with a trivial flag variation. That fails. It adds an unnecessary comment or changes a variable name in an unrelated file, runs the command again, and fails again. By turn 18, it has burned 90,000 tokens, corrupted three files that had nothing to do with the original bug, and is now arguing with its own prior reasoning traces.

Why does an LLM with billions of parameters, capable of writing complex algorithms from scratch, become remarkably stubborn when caught in a loop?

The short answer: agent loops are not random hallucinations. They are the predictable mathematical consequence of the ReAct execution pattern, autoregressive token sampling, and context window pollution.

Here is what is actually happening underneath your agent framework when an agent gets stuck, and the deterministic mechanisms required to break the cycle.

The Anatomy of the ReAct Loop

Most modern agent frameworks build on the ReAct framework, first formalized by Shunyu Yao et al. in 2022.

The core idea of ReAct is interleaving reasoning traces (Thought) and domain-specific actions (Action):

+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|                     User Task / Prompt                      |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
                               |
                               v
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| [Turn 1] LLM Generation                                     |
| Thought: I need to locate where auth tokens are validated.  |
| Action:  file_search(pattern="*auth*")                      |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
                               |
                               v
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| External Environment Execution (Bash, Tools, API)           |
| Observation: ["src/auth/jwt.py", "src/auth/middleware.py"]  |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
                               |
                               v
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| [Turn 2] LLM Context = Prompt + Turn 1 + Observation        |
| Thought: I should check middleware.py for token expiration. |
| Action:  read_file(path="src/auth/middleware.py")           |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+

Here is the critical architectural detail that gets overlooked: an LLM is completely stateless.

The model has no persistent working memory between turns. The entire state of the agent at turn N is literally the raw array of text tokens accumulated across turns 1 through N-1.

When turn 8 runs, the prompt sent over the wire looks like this:

[System Prompt]
[User Instruction]
[Turn 1: Thought -> Action -> Observation]
[Turn 2: Thought -> Action -> Observation]
...
[Turn 7: Thought -> Action -> Observation]

Every single character of past output, every bash traceback, and every failed parameter edit is fed directly into the model attention heads on every subsequent step.

The Three Mechanics That Cause the Loop

Once you understand that the context window is the sole medium for agent memory, the breakdown of long-horizon reasoning becomes easy to trace. Three distinct mechanisms drive the failure spiral.

1. In-Context Reinforcement and Autoregressive Priors

Autoregressive models predict tokens sequentially by sampling from a conditional probability distribution:

P(w_t | w_1, w_2, ..., w_{t-1})

Transformers use attention mechanisms to decide which parts of the prior sequence inform the next token. Modern models are explicitly fine-tuned on few-shot demonstrations to recognize and repeat patterns found in their context.

When an agent executes an action that fails, that failure enters the prompt history. If the agent makes a second similar attempt that also fails, the context window now contains two consecutive demonstrations of the agent executing a near-identical tool call in response to an error.

Turn 4: Action: run_command("pytest tests/test_auth.py")
        Observation: FAIL (AssertionError: expected 200, got 401)
Turn 5: Thought: Let me retry with verbose mode.
        Action: run_command("pytest -v tests/test_auth.py")
        Observation: FAIL (AssertionError: expected 200, got 401)

At Turn 6, the model attention heads attend to the repeated n-grams in the recent history. Rather than considering an orthogonal approach (such as inspecting the mock authentication fixture), the model assigns highest probability to another variation of the pytest command. The presence of repetitive actions in the context acts as an autoregressive prior that forces the model to keep repeating them.

The model is not trying to be stubborn. It is doing exactly what it was trained to do: completing the in-context pattern.

2. Context Window Poisoning

A simple tool error is manageable. Context poisoning is far more dangerous.

Context poisoning occurs when an incorrect premise or a hallucinated assumption enters the reasoning trace and is subsequently treated as ground truth by future turns.

Consider this sequence:

  1. At Turn 5, an agent runs a regex search to find a database schema file and receives empty results because its regex was slightly malformed.
  2. The agent outputs: Thought: The users table does not have an email column yet. I need to create a migration.
  3. In reality, the column already exists in migrations/0012_add_users.sql.
  4. At Turn 6, the agent writes a new migration adding the column.
  5. At Turn 7, the migration fails with duplicate column name: email.
  6. Instead of questioning its deduction from Turn 5, the agent assumes the database runner is corrupted. It attempts to rewrite the database initialization script or write custom SQL workarounds.

Because the model treats all prior tokens as factual context, it cannot easily invalidate a premise it established three turns ago. It rationalizes the conflict by inventing increasingly complex explanations for why the reality does not match its hallucinated premise.

3. The Oscillation Trap (Thrashing)

Another frequent manifestation of the agent loop is oscillation: State A -> State B -> State A -> State B.

This happens when a task has two mutually coupled constraints.

For example, a TypeScript project has a strict linter and a strict type checker.

  • The agent modifies a function to fix a linting error (such as removing an explicit any).
  • Running tsc now produces a type mismatch error.
  • The agent updates the function signature to fix the type mismatch, re-introducing the pattern flagged by the linter.
  • Running the linter throws the original lint error.

Because the ReAct loop evaluates progress only against the immediate prior observation, the agent has no memory of the global oscillation. Each local step looks like progress: "I am fixing the error that was just shown to me." Without a global diff tracker, the agent can cycle between two conflicting files until its token quota is exhausted.

The Error Recovery Paradox

Recent empirical studies on autonomous agent failure modes show how widespread this issue is.

In a benchmark analysis of over 42,000 production agent trajectories across multiple industry harnesses (such as the Wink study and MAST benchmark evaluations), researchers found that:

  • Repetitive loops and unbounded retries account for roughly 15% to 30% of all agent failures.
  • Unconstrained error recovery logic was the leading cause of runaway token consumption.

This reveals what can be termed the Error Recovery Paradox:

The code you write to handle failure is often the code that causes the agent to never stop.

When engineers build an agent harness, the instinct is to write defensive retry loops:

# The naive approach that causes loops
while not task_completed and turns < max_turns:
    thought, action = agent.predict(history)
    obs, success = execute_tool(action)
    history.append((thought, action, obs))
    # If it failed, we just feed the error right back into history

If an error is non-retryable (such as a missing system library or an invalid API token), feeding the error back to the model twenty times will produce twenty failed variations of the same command. The harness is paying API bills to watch an algorithm bang its head against a wall.

Architectural Defenses: How to Break the Failure Spiral

Breaking agent loops requires deterministic software boundaries outside the LLM. You cannot prompt your way out of context poisoning; by the time the model has entered a loop, the corrupted context makes it incapable of following prompt instructions to stop.

Here are the four deterministic defenses that robust agent runtimes use.

Defense Layer Mechanism Action on Trigger
Tool Signature Hashing SHA-256 hash of normalized (tool_name, args) Reject identical repeated calls; force alternative
N-gram Cycle Detection Sliding window over recent action signatures Detect A -> B -> A -> B oscillation patterns
Context Surgery Prune large raw stdout dumps from the message list Keep error signatures compact; avoid attention rot
State Progress Hashing Hash external environment state (git diff, test status) Abort if state remains unchanged across 3 turns

Let us look at how these work in practice.

1. Tool Call Signature Hashing

The simplest and most effective safeguard is an external tool call ledger. Before executing any tool call, compute a normalized hash of the action name and its arguments.

import hashlib
import json

def get_action_signature(tool_name: str, arguments: dict) -> str:
    # Sort keys to ensure deterministic representation
    normalized = json.dumps({"tool": tool_name, "args": arguments}, sort_keys=True)
    return hashlib.sha256(normalized.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()[:12]

If an agent attempts to invoke the exact same tool with the exact same arguments twice in a row, the harness must intercept the call before execution:

  1. Do not execute the tool.
  2. Return an explicit system warning: "Error: You have already executed this exact command with identical arguments and received result X. You are forbidden from repeating it. Formulate a different approach."

2. Detecting Multi-Step Cycles (N-gram Oscillation)

Simple equality checks only catch immediate consecutive repeats (A -> A). They miss oscillation cycles (A -> B -> A -> B or A -> B -> C -> A -> B -> C).

To catch these, maintain a rolling history of action signatures and check for repeating subsequences:

def detect_action_cycle(history: list[str], max_cycle_len: int = 3) -> bool:
    n = len(history)
    for k in range(1, max_cycle_len + 1):
        if n >= 2 * k:
            pattern = history[-k:]
            previous = history[-2*k : -k]
            if pattern == previous:
                return True
    return False

If history contains ["edit_file_a", "run_linter", "edit_file_a", "run_linter"], the detector flags a cycle of length 2 immediately on the fourth turn.

3. Context Surgery over Naive Compaction

When context windows fill up, many developers trigger an LLM summarization step. This often makes things worse. Summarization models tend to preserve high-level narrative sentences while silently discarding negative constraints (such as "never edit package.json" or specific compiler version flags).

Instead of summarizing the whole conversation with another LLM, perform deterministic context surgery:

  1. Quarantine stdout: If a terminal command returns a 4,000-line stack trace, never inject all 4,000 lines into the prompt. Write the full trace to a disk log, extract the last 15 lines and the primary error name, and pass only that excerpt to the agent.
  2. Prune failed intermediate branches: If an agent made three attempts to edit a file that resulted in syntax errors before finding a working syntax, strip the failed intermediate attempts from the history. Keep only the final valid edit. This cleanses the prompt of poisoned tokens.

Building a Lightweight Context Circuit Breaker

Here is a minimal, standalone Python implementation of a context circuit breaker that you can drop into any custom agent execution loop:

import hashlib
import json
from collections import deque
from typing import Any, Optional

class AgentCircuitBreaker:
    def __init__(self, repeat_threshold: int = 2, max_cycle_len: int = 3):
        self.repeat_threshold = repeat_threshold
        self.max_cycle_len = max_cycle_len
        self.signature_history: list[str] = []
        self.recent_calls: deque[str] = deque(maxlen=20)
        self.consecutive_repeats: int = 0
        self.last_signature: Optional[str] = None

    def _normalize(self, tool_name: str, arguments: dict[str, Any]) -> str:
        payload = {"name": tool_name.strip(), "args": arguments}
        serialized = json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True, default=str)
        return hashlib.sha256(serialized.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()[:16]

    def record_and_evaluate(self, tool_name: str, arguments: dict[str, Any]) -> tuple[bool, str]:
        sig = self._normalize(tool_name, arguments)

        # Check consecutive identical tool call
        if sig == self.last_signature:
            self.consecutive_repeats += 1
            if self.consecutive_repeats >= self.repeat_threshold:
                return False, f"Circuit Breaker Tripped: Tool '{tool_name}' invoked {self.consecutive_repeats} times with identical inputs."
        else:
            self.consecutive_repeats = 1
            self.last_signature = sig

        self.signature_history.append(sig)
        self.recent_calls.append(sig)

        # Check for oscillating n-gram cycles (e.g., A -> B -> A -> B)
        n = len(self.signature_history)
        for k in range(2, self.max_cycle_len + 1):
            if n >= 2 * k:
                recent_k = self.signature_history[-k:]
                prior_k = self.signature_history[-2 * k : -k]
                if recent_k == prior_k:
                    return False, f"Circuit Breaker Tripped: Detected repetitive cycle of length {k} in agent actions."

        return True, "OK"

When record_and_evaluate returns False, your harness should not let the agent continue blind execution.

Instead, perform an out-of-band pivot:

  1. Roll back the workspace (using git checkout or file snapshots) to the last known healthy state before the loop started.
  2. Strip the repeating cycle from the message history.
  3. Inject an out-of-band supervisor prompt: "System intervention: You were caught in a repetitive loop attempting action X. The environment has been rolled back. Action X is now locked. Identify a completely different diagnostic path."

Practical Takeaways for Agent Builders

  1. The context window is memory, not a scratchpad. Everything you feed into it shapes the model autoregressive sampling distribution. Treat context hygiene with the same discipline as database integrity.
  2. Never allow an agent to grade its own completion. Autonomous agents will cheerfully report success when tests are red if they convince themselves the test was wrong. Verification must be enforced by deterministic external tools (exit code 0, all tests pass).
  3. Prune verbosity before it reaches the model. Raw build logs and multi-megabyte API responses do not give the model more intelligence. They dilute attention heads and accelerate context poisoning.
  4. Enforce hard stopping criteria. A maximum turn limit is a fallback of last resort. Use tool signature hashing, cycle detection, and progress checks to halt runaway agents in 3 turns rather than 30.

articles.title: I Built a macOS Assistant - Bhai, Then Realized I Was Solving the Wrong Problem
articles.description: An experiment with local-first software, AI coding agents, shared memory, and the strange habit of...
articles.body_html:
An experiment with local-first software, AI coding agents, shared memory, and the strange habit of building things just to see if they can work.

It started with a very ordinary frustration.

I was working on a project, switching between my editor, terminal, browser, and a coding agent. Nothing unusual. Just another day of development.

At some point, I found myself repeating something I had already explained.

The project structure. A decision we'd made earlier. What had already been implemented. What was still pending.

And I remember thinking:

Why am I explaining this again?

Not because explaining things is difficult. But because the information already existed somewhere. In an earlier conversation, a terminal session, a document, or simply in my head.

Yet every time I switched tools, some part of that context seemed to disappear.

That was the tiny frustration that started this experiment.

I didn't have a business idea. I wasn't trying to build the next developer productivity tool.

I just wanted to see if I could make my Mac a little more aware of what I was doing.

So I started building something I called Bhai.

Yes, Bhai. Because naming a serious developer tool something completely unserious felt appropriate.

It Was Supposed to Be a Small Thing

The original idea was straightforward.

What if I could type something like:

bhai memory dekh

And get useful information about my Mac?

Or ask Bhai to open a project, inspect its Git status, or help with the small repetitive tasks that come with development?

I didn't want another chatbot connected to an API.

I wanted something local. Fast. Predictable. Something that could understand a handful of commands and execute them without needing an LLM to interpret every sentence.

So I started with Electron, React, TypeScript, and SQLite.

A small macOS menu-bar application. A floating panel. Some deterministic commands. Local storage.

Nothing particularly revolutionary.

And for a while, that was the entire plan.

But building side projects has a funny way of changing the questions you're trying to answer.

The more I worked on Bhai, the less interested I became in asking it to check my RAM.

Something else was bothering me.

Why Does Every AI Agent Feel Like a New Colleague on Their First Day?

I'd been experimenting with different AI coding agents.

Claude Code for one task. Codex for another. Sometimes an agent inside an editor.

They're all capable tools, but there's a frustrating moment when you move from one to another.

The new agent often needs to understand things the previous agent already figured out.

Why a certain approach was rejected.

Which files were changed.

What broke during testing.

Which architectural decision should not be revisited.

What work remains unfinished.

Of course, there are ways around this.

You can maintain an AGENTS.md file. Write documentation. Create handoff notes. Give the new agent a detailed prompt.

But I kept coming back to one question:

What if project context didn't belong to any individual AI agent?

What if it belonged to the project itself?

And every agent could contribute to it?

That idea was much more interesting to me than a macOS command assistant.

So Bhai slowly became something else.

Giving Different Agents a Shared Notebook

I started experimenting with a local project memory system.

The concept was simple.

Imagine Claude Code is working on an authentication feature.

During the session, it discovers an important constraint, makes an architectural decision, modifies some files, and encounters a blocker.

Instead of leaving that information buried in a conversation, it can record a few structured checkpoints.

Something like:

Authentication middleware implemented.

Existing session validation must remain backward-compatible.

Unit tests passed. Protected-route integration tests are still pending.

Later, I open Codex.

Codex asks Bhai for the latest project context, retrieves the previous handoff, and can see where the work stopped.

The idea is not to make one agent remember another agent's entire conversation.

It's to give both agents access to a small, durable record of what matters.

I used the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect the agents to Bhai.

Underneath, it's a local SQLite database, a permission-controlled MCP bridge, and a set of tools for reading and contributing project knowledge.

I also gave the MCP tools slightly ridiculous Romanized-Hinglish names.

yebata — tell me the relevant context.

yesavekar — save this checkpoint.

kahanthe — where did we leave off?

yaadrakh — remember this decision.

I could have used conventional names.

But honestly, where's the fun in that?

The underlying operations still have precise contracts. The unusual names are just part of Bhai's personality.

Then Came the Memory Problem

Once agents could write checkpoints, another question appeared.

What happens after a hundred checkpoints?

Or five hundred?

If Bhai simply collects everything and sends it to the next agent, I've recreated the same problem I was trying to solve.

Too much context.

Too much repetition.

Too many historical details that might no longer matter.

So I started building a deterministic context-compaction layer.

The goal was to reduce redundant information without throwing away things that should remain important.

Repeated progress updates could be merged.

Architectural decisions needed to survive.

Unresolved blockers needed to remain visible.

Conflicting claims couldn't simply overwrite each other.

If one agent claimed a service used port 5001 and another claimed 5002, Bhai shouldn't silently pick the latest answer and pretend it was a verified fact.

It should preserve that uncertainty.

I also experimented with three different context sizes:

  • Quick: Just enough to orient an agent.
  • Task: The relevant details for the current work.
  • Deep: More comprehensive architectural and historical context.

The entire process could work without a cloud LLM.

I explored optional local-model assistance, but the deterministic layer was always supposed to work by itself.

That was an important constraint for me.

I wanted Bhai to remain useful even when the internet wasn't available.

A Result That Looked Almost Too Good

At one point, I ran a synthetic compaction experiment involving 100 checkpoints.

The raw checkpoint history was estimated at approximately 6,985 tokens.

After compaction, it was around 594 tokens.

That's roughly a 91% reduction in the amount of checkpoint text.

My first reaction was pretty much:

Okay, that's interesting.

But then I started questioning what that number actually meant.

Did it prove an AI coding agent would use 91% fewer tokens?

No.

Did it prove that the compacted context preserved everything an agent would need?

Not necessarily.

Was the benchmark representative of a real project, with messy context, outdated assumptions, and incomplete documentation?

Not yet.

And this distinction matters.

Compressing information is relatively easy. Compressing information without losing what matters is the actual problem.

The result was encouraging, but it wasn't proof of better real-world coding-agent performance.

That would require actual tasks, real agent sessions, and comparisons against approaches like AGENTS.md and ordinary repository exploration.

It was a good reminder not to confuse an impressive benchmark with a solved problem.

I Kept Building Anyway

By this point, Bhai had grown well beyond its original purpose.

There was a local memory engine, structured checkpoints, architectural decisions, tasks, handoffs, context packs, agent permissions, and a desktop interface to browse everything.

I had also spent time thinking about process supervision, local developer services, and restoring development environments.

The architecture was becoming more sophisticated.

But something strange was happening.

Every time I finished one feature, I could think of three more.

And every time I asked myself what made Bhai genuinely different from existing tools, I struggled to give a convincing answer.

Sure, individual pieces were useful.

But was the complete experience compelling enough that another developer would install and keep using it?

I didn't know.

And I realized I had spent much more time answering:

Can I build this?

Than asking:

Does this actually need to exist?

Those are two very different questions.

The Hardest Part Wasn't Technical

The technical problems were interesting.

How do you isolate local processes safely?

How do you prevent MCP clients from accessing projects they aren't authorized to use?

How do you preserve decisions without accumulating endless context?

How do you distinguish agent-reported claims from verified facts?

How do you keep the whole system local-first?

Each problem had trade-offs I enjoyed thinking through.

But the most difficult question was surprisingly nontechnical.

Why would someone choose Bhai over the tools they already have?

I had built pieces of a developer assistant.

I hadn't yet discovered its defining reason to exist.

There's a temptation at this point to keep building.

Maybe the next feature will make everything click.

Maybe adding workflows will solve it.

Maybe restoring an entire development workspace will finally make the product feel complete.

And sometimes that approach works.

But I didn't want to keep expanding the project just because I'd already invested time in it.

So I decided to pause.

Not because the experiment failed.

And not because I regret building it.

I just felt that the next thing I needed wasn't another implementation phase.

It was a better understanding of the problem.

What I Actually Got Out of It

Looking back, I learned more from this experiment than I expected.

I got to explore local-first application architecture, Electron's process boundaries, SQLite persistence, MCP integrations, structured agent memory, context compaction, and a surprising number of security and reliability edge cases.

But there were a few lessons that stayed with me.

First, shared memory and shared understanding aren't the same thing.

Two agents having access to the same information doesn't guarantee they'll interpret it correctly.

Second, less context doesn't always mean better context.

A concise handoff is valuable only if the information that was removed wasn't necessary.

Third, infrastructure can be technically useful without being a compelling product.

That's probably the biggest lesson for me.

And finally, I was reminded that experimentation doesn't always need to end with a launch.

Sometimes you build something because a question bothers you.

You explore it, learn from it, and move on.

That's a perfectly reasonable outcome.

If You're Curious, Here's Bhai

I've also put together a small website for Bhai and open-sourced the project.

If you're curious about what I built, how it works, or just want to explore the code:

🌐 Website: https://hi-bhai.vercel.app/

💻 GitHub: https://github.com/vibhanshu2001/bh-ai

It's an experiment, not a polished commercial product. There are rough edges, unfinished ideas, and probably a few things I'd do differently if I started over.

But that's the fun of building in public. Someone else might find an interesting idea in something you've decided to leave unfinished.

One Question I'm Still Curious About

I haven't ruled out returning to Bhai someday.

But for now, I'm leaving it where it is.

There's still one question I genuinely want to explore:

When you switch between Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or other AI coding agents, how do you preserve the context of what you've already done?

Do you maintain an AGENTS.md file?

Do you rely on each agent's built-in memory or session history?

Do you use an MCP memory server?

Or do you just explain everything again and get on with it?

I'm particularly curious whether cross-agent context loss is something other developers actually struggle with—or whether I've spent a lot of time solving a problem that's mostly in my own workflow.

Either answer would be useful.

And that's probably what I like most about experiments.

You don't always need to know what you're building toward.

Sometimes curiosity is enough to get started.

Bhai started as a small personal experiment, grew into something much more complex, and is now open-source. I'm sharing it not because I've solved the problem, but because I enjoyed exploring it—and maybe someone else will find something useful in the journey.

articles.title: A Lang Graph Timeout Doesn't Undo Your Charge: The Retry Trap in 1.2
