articles.body_html:
What happens to a payment that succeeds 200 milliseconds after your timeout fires?

Your graph state says nothing happened. Your payment provider says it charged the card. And LangGraph, following its defaults, is about to charge it again.

Per-node timeouts and node-level error handlers arrived in langgraph 1.2 (they require langgraph>=1.2), and most of the attention went to the features themselves. The more interesting part is how a timeout interacts with retries and side effects, because the combination is easy to misconfigure.

The code in this article is illustrative. payments, State and fetch_batches are stand-ins for your own provider client, state schema and data source.

The scenario

A checkout agent has a node that charges the customer. Providers occasionally stall, so you do the responsible thing and cap the node:


from langgraph.types import RetryPolicy, TimeoutPolicy

async def charge_customer(state: State) -> dict:
    charge = await payments.create_charge(
        customer_id=state["customer_id"],
        amount=state["amount"],
    )
    return {"charge_id": charge.id}

builder.add_node(
    "charge_customer",
    charge_customer,
    timeout=TimeoutPolicy(run_timeout=10),
    retry_policy=RetryPolicy(max_attempts=3),
)

Reasonable on its face. Here is what the docs say happens when attempt one takes 11 seconds:

LangGraph raises NodeTimeoutError and clears any writes from that attempt.
NodeTimeoutError is retryable by default, so the retry policy re-runs the node from the top.
If your provider committed the first charge at second 10.2, attempt two charges again.
Why it works this way

LangGraph gives you three mechanisms that compose in a fixed order. An attempt raises an exception, and a timeout is just one more exception. The retry policy decides whether to go again. Only after retries are exhausted does the error_handler run.

State stays correct because checkpoints are written at super-step boundaries, not mid-function, and writes from a failed attempt are discarded. That guarantee covers the graph. It does not cover the outside world. The fault-tolerance docs are explicit that retries give at-least-once semantics for node execution, and that payments, emails and external writes sit outside the checkpoint boundary.

So the timeout does what it says: it clears graph state. It can't clear a charge.

Retries also multiply your worst case. The timeout clock resets on every attempt, so three attempts at a 10-second run_timeout can hold the node for about 30 seconds plus backoff. The defaults are a 0.5 s initial interval, a factor of 2, and jitter. That's my arithmetic, not a documented number, but it's worth checking against your own latency budget.

Making the node safe to repeat

The fix isn't a smarter timeout. It's making repeat execution harmless, and the docs give a specific rule for that: the idempotency key must be derivable from state that is already durable. Generating a UUID inside the node fails, because if the process dies before the node returns, the key was never checkpointed and the retry mints a new one.


from langgraph.errors import NodeError, NodeTimeoutError
from langgraph.types import Command, RetryPolicy, TimeoutPolicy

async def charge_customer(state: State) -> dict:
    key = f"charge:{state['order_id']}"          # stable across retries and resumes
    charge = await payments.create_charge(
        customer_id=state["customer_id"],
        amount=state["amount"],
        idempotency_key=key,
    )
    return {"charge_id": charge.id}

def route_charge_failure(state: State, error: NodeError) -> Command:
    timed_out = isinstance(error.error, NodeTimeoutError)
    return Command(
        update={"charge_outcome": "unknown" if timed_out else "failed"},
        goto="reconcile_payment",
    )

async def reconcile_payment(state: State) -> dict:
    # A missing acknowledgement is "unknown", not "didn't happen".
    status = await payments.lookup(f"charge:{state['order_id']}")
    return {"charge_outcome": status}

builder.add_node(
    "charge_customer",
    charge_customer,
    timeout=TimeoutPolicy(run_timeout=15),
    retry_policy=RetryPolicy(max_attempts=3),
    error_handler=route_charge_failure,
)
builder.add_node("reconcile_payment", reconcile_payment)

Two details matter. The key comes from order_id, which already lives in state. And the error handler doesn't guess. It routes to a node whose only job is to ask the provider what actually happened, which matches the docs' advice to treat missing local state as unknown and query the provider before compensating.

The handler gets NodeError injected by type annotation, so you can tell a timeout from a declined card without parsing strings.

The idle timeout has a blind spot

TimeoutPolicy has two limits. run_timeout is a hard wall-clock cap that never refreshes. idle_timeout resets whenever the node shows progress, and under the default refresh_on="auto" the list of things that count as progress is long: state writes, streamed chunks, child-task scheduling, stream-writer calls, and any LangChain callback event from the node or its descendants, including LLM tokens and tool calls.

That's the right default for a node wrapping an agent loop. It also means a node that is spinning, say retrying a flaky tool in a loop while a sub-chain keeps emitting callbacks, can look healthy to the idle clock indefinitely. If you want "idle" to mean "my code said it's alive", narrow it:


from langgraph.runtime import Runtime

async def ingest(state: State, runtime: Runtime) -> dict:
    async for batch in fetch_batches():
        await process(batch)
        runtime.heartbeat()          # the only thing that resets the clock
    return {"status": "done"}

builder.add_node(
    "ingest",
    ingest,
    timeout=TimeoutPolicy(idle_timeout=30, refresh_on="heartbeat"),
)

runtime.heartbeat() is a no-op outside an idle-timed attempt, so it's safe to leave in unconditionally. If you fan out with Send, you can also override the timeout per push, which is handy for tightening it on individual items.

Trade-offs and edges
Async only. A sync node with timeout= is rejected at compile time, because sync Python can't be safely cancelled in-process. The docs suggest asyncio.to_thread for blocking I/O. Keep in mind, as general Python behaviour rather than anything LangGraph-specific, that cancelling the awaiting coroutine doesn't stop the thread. The blocking call can keep running after the timeout has "fired".
Interrupts bypass all of this. interrupt() raises through GraphBubbleUp, so it skips both retry policies and error handlers. Human-in-the-loop pauses won't trigger your compensation logic.
One handler per node, and if the handler raises, the exception bubbles as if there were no handler.
set_node_defaults isn't inherited by subgraphs. Each graph needs its own, so a timeout you set at the top level won't protect a nested graph.
Idempotency depends on the provider. The key only helps if the service honours it. Check before relying on it, and for effects that can't be made idempotent, the docs suggest moving them out of retryable nodes.
My take

The feature everyone expects from "timeouts" is a stuck agent that gets unstuck. What 1.2 actually ships is a more honest model of failure: the graph is transactional at the super-step level, the world isn't, and the gap between them is your problem. The docs say so plainly, which I appreciate.

I used to file a node timeout under reliability features. I now think of it as a switch that turns slow failures into retries, and retries are only reliable if the work inside them is safe to repeat. Add a timeout to a node with side effects and you've made a decision about duplicates, whether or not you wrote it down.

So the real review question for any node you wrap with timeout= is whether running it twice is harmless. If the answer is "I'd have to check", the timeout isn't ready.

Which of your nodes would do real damage if they ran twice, and do they have a key that survives a crash?

References
LangGraph docs, Fault tolerance (retries, timeouts, error handlers, idempotency, graceful shutdown)
LangGraph docs, Graph API nodes (node timeouts, set_node_defaults)
LangGraph Python changelog (v1.2 release notes)
API reference, NodeTimeoutError

articles.title: Converting Centimeters to Inches Without Pretending Rounded Results Are Exact
articles.description: One inch is exactly 2.54 centimeters, but that does not make every centimeter-to-inch result an exact...
articles.body_html:
One inch is exactly 2.54 centimeters, but that does not make every centimeter-to-inch result an exact decimal. I wanted a small conversion page to make that distinction clear: an exact unit definition, a floating-point calculation, and a rounded display are three different things.

This matters when you build a measurement UI. The usual multiplication or division is easy; deciding how many digits to show, what a reverse conversion means, and whether a tiny measurement should disappear is where the numerical contract actually takes shape.

Use Exact Definitions Without Duplicating Pair Formulas

The conversion page uses the same helper as the site's general length converter. Instead of storing a formula for each direction, the helper gives each supported unit a scale relative to meters.

The relevant entries are cm: 0.01 and inch: 0.0254. The actual conversion function is:

export function convertLength(value, fromKey, toKey) {
  const meters = (Number(value) || 0) * (lengthUnitMap[fromKey] || 0);
  return lengthUnitMap[toKey] ? meters / lengthUnitMap[toKey] : 0;
}

For centimeters to inches, it multiplies the input by 0.01 and divides by 0.0254. Algebraically, that is the familiar division by 2.54.

The useful design decision is not making the arithmetic shorter. It is having one unit table serve both the general converter and the fixed-pair page. Correcting a scale or adding a supported unit should not require hunting through many slightly different copies of the same formula.

The inch definition itself is exact. A rounded reciprocal such as 0.3937 inches per centimeter is an approximation, so repeatedly using that shortened multiplier introduces an avoidable source of error before display rounding even begins.

The helper does not use a decimal-arithmetic library, however. Its constants and operations are JavaScript Number values, so the exact definition is still evaluated through binary floating-point arithmetic.

An Exact Constant Does Not Mean an Exact Binary Fraction

Most decimal fractions do not have a finite representation in binary. The same issue that makes 0.1 + 0.2 surprising also applies to ordinary measurement constants.

That does not make JavaScript unusable for a household measurement converter. It means the presentation should not confuse a long sequence of digits with certainty, or assume two algebraically equivalent expressions must produce bit-for-bit identical intermediate results.

The shared helper rounds its output as follows:

export function roundLengthResult(v) {
  if (!isFinite(v)) return 0;
  return Math.round(v * 1e6) / 1e6;
}

For 100 centimeters, the displayed result is 39.370079 inches. For 2.54 centimeters, it is 1 inch. Those are sensible outputs for the page's six-decimal policy.

Notice what the function returns: a number, not a string padded to six decimal places. A result of 1 is displayed as 1, not necessarily 1.000000. “At most six decimal places” is a different promise from “always show six places.”

The limit also concerns decimal places, not significant figures. A value close to zero can lose a much larger proportion of its information than a large value. A single display policy is convenient, but it is not a complete scientific measurement policy.

I would keep input precision, calculation precision, and display precision separate when reviewing a numeric interface. A precise-looking display cannot recover uncertainty in a ruler reading, and rounding output should not be described as increasing the accuracy of the original measurement.

Round Trips Can Lose Information

The fixed-pair page lets the user edit either side. Its left-to-right synchronization writes a rounded output:

toValue.value = categoryConfig.value.round(
  categoryConfig.value.convert(fromValue.value, pair.value.from, pair.value.to),
);

The reverse direction uses the corresponding reverse conversion. A synchronization guard prevents the programmatically written output from immediately rewriting the original input.

That protects the current editing direction, but it does not make rounding invertible. If the user later edits or copies the rounded inch result, that rounded number becomes the next input. Information discarded from the earlier result is no longer available.

A particularly clear boundary is 0.000001 centimeters. Converted to inches, it is about 0.0000003937 before display rounding. The six-decimal helper returns zero. Converting that zero back produces zero centimeters, not the original tiny measurement.

This is quantization, not evidence that the unit factor is wrong. Many different small inputs map to the same displayed number, so no reverse operation can identify which original value produced it.

For tests, I would check representative values with an explicitly chosen tolerance rather than asserting exact equality for every arbitrary round trip. I would also include a tiny input that intentionally rounds to zero. That test documents the actual output contract instead of treating the loss as an unexpected accident.

For ordinary nonnegative values, I can estimate that tolerance from the two rounding steps. Rounding inches to six decimal places contributes at most 0.0000005 inch, or 0.00000127 centimeters. Rounding the reverse result adds at most 0.0000005 centimeters, giving a combined absolute error budget of 0.00000177 centimeters, before allowing for floating-point error. That is a display-rounding budget, not a guarantee about the original measurement's accuracy or extreme numeric inputs.

Unit Conversion Does Not Interpret the Measurement

The page's English content discusses heights and screen sizes. The underlying function only converts a scalar length; it does not know what was measured.

A screen measurement in inches generally describes the diagonal. Converting that diagonal to centimeters does not tell you the display's width or height without an aspect ratio. Similarly, a number of inches is not automatically a feet-and-inches height string.

The rounding helper returns zero when its incoming, unrounded result is nonfinite. That check happens before multiplication by one million: a sufficiently large finite result can still overflow during rounding and return Infinity. For example, converting 1e308 centimeters produces a finite intermediate result, but rounding it overflows. The function does not recheck after scaling.

Input handling is a separate boundary. Both fields use type="number", v-model.number, and min="0". On blur, validateInput checks whether the value converts to a finite, nonnegative number and resets an invalid field to zero. That validation does not run before every conversion. The conversion helper itself also coerces nonnumeric input to zero, so these fallbacks do not establish that every displayed zero represents a genuine zero-length measurement.

For ordinary sizing comparisons, the implementation is useful precisely because its scope is small. For engineering tolerances, explicit error states, locale-aware parsing, or preservation of significant figures, I would define a stricter numeric model rather than silently extending the meaning of this one.

I turned this conversion and its shared rounding policy into a small free tool: CM to Inches Converter.

articles.title: An offline write queue for React Native, and the two reader questions that changed it
articles.description: Short answer: Bareship queues offline writes with TanStack Query: a paused mutation is saved to MMKV,...
articles.body_html:
Short answer: Bareship queues offline writes with TanStack Query: a paused mutation is saved to MMKV, so it survives the app being killed, and replays in order when the phone reconnects. Every write gets an Idempotency-Key when the user taps, reused for every attempt, so the server applies it once. Since 0.4.0, each write also records the account that made it and is never sent for anyone else, and a write can cancel the dependent writes queued behind it if the server rejects it.

In the launch post I said Bareship saves a like made offline, keeps it through a
restart and sends it once when the phone reconnects, and promised the next post would show how.

Two readers on dev.to then asked questions I hadn't fully answered. Dave Kurian
asked whose write it is when someone else signs in before it's sent. Odd Eggs Studio
asked what happens to the writes behind one the server rejects. Both answers are now code, released in
0.4.0. This post walks through the queue from the tap
to the server, with those two changes in the places they belong.

What can go wrong with one like

Someone likes a post on a train with no signal. Before that like reaches your server, any of these can happen:

  1. The user swipes the app away, or the OS kills it.
  2. The request goes out, the connection drops before the answer comes back, and the app tries again. Now the server has seen it twice.
  3. They like, then unlike. The two requests arrive in the wrong order.
  4. They sign out and someone else signs in on the same phone. The like is still waiting.
  5. The server refuses the like for good, and three edits that depend on it are queued behind it.

A queue that only handles the first one still looks fine in a demo. The other four show up later, in bug reports
you can't reproduce. (For the wider design questions, such as a local database, conflicts and photo uploads, see my
offline-first data layer post. This one is about the write queue
only.)

The base: TanStack Query, with the gaps filled

Bareship doesn't have its own queue engine. TanStack Query already does most of the work:

  • A mutation with networkMode: 'online' pauses while the phone is offline instead of failing, and resumes when the connection returns.
  • Paused mutations can be saved with the query cache. Bareship stores that cache in MMKV, so a waiting write survives the app being killed.
  • Mutations that share a scope run one at a time, in the order they were made. That handles problem 3.

The gap is in what gets saved. A restored mutation is only data: its key and its variables. The functions that
send it and update the screen aren't saved, because you can't save a function. TanStack Query looks them up by
the mutation's key in the defaults registered on the client. If nothing is registered yet when the saved cache
comes back, the write fails with "No mutationFn found".

In React Native that's easy to get wrong. Metro loads modules lazily, so the feature that defines the like may not
have run yet when the cache is restored at startup. Bareship fixes this with one file, src/app/queued-writes.ts,
which imports every module that defines a queued write and is imported before the cache is restored. A test fails
if a definition is missing from it. A write whose definition really is gone, say removed in an app update, is
dropped and logged at startup instead of crashing.

From the feature's side, a queued write is one definition at module level:

src/features/feed/api.ts

const likeKey = ['posts', 'like'] as const;

export const useToggleLike = defineQueuedMutation<Post, { postId: string; like: boolean }>({
  mutationKey: likeKey,
  mutationFn: ({ postId, like, idempotencyKey }) => {
    const url = `/posts/${encodeURIComponent(postId)}/like`;
    return like
      ? http.post(url, PostSchema, { idempotencyKey })
      : http.delete(url, PostSchema, { idempotencyKey });
  },
  onMutate: async ({ postId, like }) => {
    await queryClient.cancelQueries({ queryKey: postKeys.all });
    updatePost(queryClient, postId, applyLike(like)); // show it at once
  },
  onError: (_error, { postId, like }) => {
    updatePost(queryClient, postId, applyLike(!like)); // undo it
    toast.error(i18n.t('feed.likeFailed'));
  },
  onSuccess: (updated, { postId }) => {
    // A like then an unlike queued offline: keep the optimistic state until the last one lands.
    if (hasLaterWrite(likeKey, variables => variables.postId === postId)) return;
    updatePost(queryClient, updated.id, () => updated);
  },
});

The cache work lives in these callbacks, not in the screen, because after a restart the screen that started the
write is gone. The variables are saved as JSON, so they stay small: ids and flags, not whole objects.

The "Waiting to sync" label comes from the paused writes themselves. useWaitingWrites(likeKey) returns the
variables of every like still waiting, and the banner under the header counts them. Nothing is tracked twice.

Sent twice, applied once: idempotency keys

Problem 2 can't be solved on the phone alone. If the connection drops after the server got the request, the app
can't know whether the like landed. It has to try again, so the server has to recognise a repeat.

Every queued write gets an Idempotency-Key (a random UUID) when the user taps, not when the request is sent.
That one key goes with every attempt:

  • The HTTP client retries network errors, timeouts, 408, 429 and 5xx with backoff, up to 3 attempts in all. It reuses the key each time.
  • A write replayed after a restart reuses the key.
  • A write the server already answered is never sent again.

On the server, the rule is to store the first response for each key and return it for repeats. Here's the mock
backend that ships with the template, which does exactly that for likes:

src/mocks/handlers.ts

const key = request.headers.get('Idempotency-Key');
const replay = key ? db.idempotency.get(key) : undefined;
if (replay) return HttpResponse.json(replay); // seen it: same answer, applied once

// ...apply the like...
const body = postDto(post, user.id);
if (key) db.idempotency.set(key, body);
return HttpResponse.json(body);

One limit, written down in the code: a write that's already on the wire when the app dies isn't saved, because
it's no longer paused. Its key still makes a manual retry safe.

Question 1: whose write is it?

Dave's question was about problem 4. A like is queued, the user signs out, someone else signs in, the phone
reconnects. Does the first user's like go out with the second user's token?

My answer at the time was "no, because sign-out clears the queue". That was true, but the guarantee lived in the
sign-out flow. Any future change there, like account switching or a sign-out that fails halfway, could break it
without anyone noticing. Dave suggested storing the account next to the key, and he was right.

Now each write records who made it:

src/data/offline.ts

mutate: variables =>
  mutation.mutate({ ...variables, idempotencyKey: createId(), accountId: currentAccount() }),

It's checked twice. The first check is when the saved queue comes back after a restart. The second is just before
each write is sent, because the account can change while a write waits offline:

src/data/offline.ts

mutationFn: variables => {
  if (!belongsToCurrentAccount(variables)) throw new OtherAccountWriteError();
  return mutationFn(variables);
},

A write from another account is dropped and logged. It never reaches the server, and it doesn't call the
feature's onError, so the new user doesn't see someone else's rollback or error message. Writes saved by older
versions have no account id and replay as before.

The server side matters too: keep idempotency keys per user, so a replayed key can never match another account's
record. That's now in the docs.

Question 2: what if the server says no?

Odd Eggs Studio asked about problem 5. If a queued write is rejected, does the queue stop or carry on?

It carries on, and for likes that's right: each like stands alone, so one refused like shouldn't block the next.
But some writes depend on each other. "Create a draft, then edit it" is the usual example. If the create fails,
sending the edit only produces a second error, and the screen is left showing a draft that doesn't exist.

So defineQueuedMutation now takes onRejected:

src/features/drafts/api.ts

export const useCreateDraft = defineQueuedMutation<Draft, { draftId: string; title: string }>({
  mutationKey: ['drafts', 'create'],
  scope: 'drafts',
  onRejected: 'cancel-scope', // if this fails for good, drop the drafts writes queued behind it
  mutationFn: …,
});

export const useEditDraft = defineQueuedMutation<Draft, { draftId: string; body: string }>({
  mutationKey: ['drafts', 'edit'],
  scope: 'drafts',
  mutationFn: …,
  onError: (error, { draftId }) => {
    // Runs for a cancelled edit too (error.kind === 'cancelled'): undo its optimistic update.
  },
});

The details that took the most thought:

  • "Fails for good" means the server refused the write, or it still failed after the HTTP client's retries. Going offline isn't a failure: the queue just pauses.
  • Each cancelled write gets its own onError, with an error of kind 'cancelled'. Every write rolls back its own optimistic update, so the screen ends up correct without the failed write having to know what came after it.
  • Only writes already queued are cancelled. Something the user does after the failure runs normally.
  • The limit: if the app is killed between the failure and the next launch, the cancellation isn't remembered. The writes behind it go out and fail on their own, as they did before. I wrote this down in the docs instead of adding more machinery for a rare case.

What I took from this

Both changes came from comments on a launch post. Each one turned into an issue, a change with tests, a docs
section and a release. Two things stood out to me:

  • Put a guarantee in the data, not in a flow. "Sign-out clears the queue" was true, but it depended on code far from the queue. "Every write knows its account" stays true whatever happens elsewhere.
  • Default to the simple behaviour, and make the strict one a single line. Most writes are independent, so 'continue' stays the default. The chains that need more get 'cancel-scope', and the limit is written next to it.

Try it 

npx create-bareship Acme
cd Acme
pnpm android   # or: pnpm ios

Sign in with demo@example.com / password123, turn on airplane mode, like a post, close the app, open it again,
then turn airplane mode off. The like is sent once. The mock backend runs inside the app, so you don't need a
server for any of this.

  • Queue code: src/data/offline.ts
  • Guide: Offline and writes that depend on each other
  • The two changes: #28 (account) and #29 (onRejected)

Next in the series: an architecture the linter enforces. Layers and feature boundaries that ESLint checks, so
code review doesn't have to.

If you have a question like Dave's or Odd Eggs Studio's, leave it in the comments on dev.to or open an issue. Two of
them have already made the template better.

FAQ

How does Bareship keep offline writes after the app is killed?

Queued writes are TanStack Query mutations that pause while offline. Paused mutations are saved with the query
cache in MMKV and replayed in order on the next launch, once every write's definition is registered.

How does Bareship stop a write from being applied twice?

Each write gets an Idempotency-Key when the user taps, and every retry or replay sends the same key. The server
stores the first response for each key and returns it for repeats.

Can a queued write be sent under another user's account?

No. Since 0.4.0 each write records the account that made it, and it's checked on restore and before every send.
A write from another account is dropped and logged, without calling the feature's error handler.

Takeaways

  • Bareship's offline queue is TanStack Query paused mutations, saved to MMKV and replayed in order after a restart.
  • Register every queued write's definition before the saved cache is restored: Metro loads modules lazily.
  • One Idempotency-Key per write, made when the user taps and reused for every attempt, so the server applies it once.
  • Each queued write records its account and is checked on restore and before every send (0.4.0).
  • onRejected: 'cancel-scope' drops the dependent writes behind a rejected one, and each rolls back its own update.

I write about React Native in practice, measured and with public code, at praveensingh.co.in/blog.

articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge.

What I Built

Ma (間) is a small desktop teleprompter for practising a talk, a pitch or an interview answer.

Most rehearsal tools time your words. Ma watches the thing that actually derails a talk: you speed up when your body speeds up. It reads your pulse and breathing from the webcam with the SmartSpectra SDK and uses them in two ways.

  1. While you rehearse. Ma first takes a 30-second calm reference while you sit still. Then you read your script line by line and press Space for the next one. When your pulse climbs 10 bpm or your breathing climbs 5 breaths/min above your own reference, Ma holds the next line and asks for one slow breath. It watches the chest trace and releases the line as soon as it sees that breath (or after 9 seconds, so you are never stuck).
  2. Afterwards. Ma shows the script again with a heat bar on every line for how far your pulse ran above your reference, how much of the line you were talking, your blink rate, and a short list of "plan a pause here" spots for the next run.

"Ma" is the Japanese word for the pause that gives rhythm to speech. The app is built around one idea: the pause is part of the talk, and your body tells you where it belongs.

Demo

Video (1 min 49 s): https://github.com/Class-now/pace-prompter/releases/download/v1.0.0/ma-demo.mp4

The video is a real rehearsal with a live webcam and the live SmartSpectra readings: the opt-in screen, the 30-second calm reference (shown at 5x speed), three breath pauses triggered when breathing ran above my own reference, and the review screen at the end. The face is blurred with Ma's own preview option, and the video has no sound; captions explain each step.

Code

https://github.com/Class-now/pace-prompter

  • Electron app, plain JavaScript, @smartspectra/node-sdk 3.4.0
  • src/core.js holds the pacing logic with no DOM or SDK dependency and is covered by npm test
  • test/sdk-smoke.mjs is a headless check against the real SDK: it pushes a recorded face video through useCustomInput() / sendFrame() and passes when pulse and breathing readings appear
  • Setup: npm install, put SMARTSPECTRA_API_KEY=... in .env, npm start

How It Responds to Human Signals

SmartSpectra signal What Ma does with it
cardio.pulseRate calm reference during calibration; live readout; breath-pause trigger (+10 bpm over your reference); per-line heat in the review
breathing.rate calm reference; breath-pause trigger (+5 breaths/min over your reference)
breathing.upperTrace drawn as the live breath line; detects the one full breath that releases a pause
face.talking shows whether you are speaking; share of each line spent talking
face.blinking blinks per minute per line in the review

Every comparison is against the same person's reading from a minute earlier, never against a population norm. A pulse of 95 means nothing on its own; a pulse that jumped from 72 to 90 in the middle of your second paragraph is exactly what you want to know before you give the talk for real. Ma also reads the SDK's validation status ("Hold still", "Face the camera", "Only one face is allowed") and shows it under the preview, so you can fix your framing before the calm reference is taken.

Consent and Data Handling

  • Opt-in every time. Nothing starts until you tick the consent box on the first screen, which says what is measured and why. The camera light is on only between Start and the review screen.
  • Camera only. Ma never requests the microphone. The app's permission handler refuses every permission except video for its own local page.
  • What leaves the machine. The SmartSpectra SDK reaches Presage's service with your API key to produce measurements. Ma turns the SDK's optional usage telemetry off (enableTelemetry: false). Ma itself has no server and sends nothing anywhere.
  • What is stored. Nothing. Video frames are never written to disk. The numbers for the current run live in memory and are gone when you close the window or start again. The only way a result leaves the app is the Copy report button, which puts a Markdown summary on your clipboard.
  • Who is measured. Only the person who started the session and is sitting in front of the camera. Ma is built for self-rehearsal.
  • No health claims. Readings are shown as pacing notes relative to your own resting reference, never as a judgement about health or emotion. Ma is not a medical device.

Agent Session

I built Ma with Claude Code as a pair: I described the rehearsal problem and the "compare only with yourself" rule, and the agent wrote the pacing logic and tests first, then the Electron shell and SDK wiring. One thing the agent found along the way: on Windows the SDK's useFile() input reports kInputUnavailable, so the headless test pushes frames through useCustomInput() / sendFrame() instead, which is the same path the app uses for the camera.

articles.description: Web Models API: Practical Guide   In the last article, I focused on why I think an API that...
articles.body_html:
Web Models API: Practical Guide

In the last article, I focused on why I think an API that exposes open-weight, on-device models to web apps is desperately needed, and why the Web Models API could be a good solution.

In this article, I want to get down to brass tacks and show what the code would look like. I'll focus on the developer's side. I'll write more about how the browser implementation works in a future article.

These examples follow the current proposal. The API is still being developed and may change.

The API

Before getting into the examples, here's the API at a glance:

// Request access to a model.
navigator.models.requestAccess(model);

// Generate text, stream a response, or create embeddings.
navigator.models.generate(model, input);
navigator.models.stream(model, input);
navigator.models.embed(model, input);

// Bind a model for repeated calls.
navigator.models.session(model);

// Read model details after access has been granted.
navigator.models.info(model);
navigator.models.list();

For a more extensive look at the input and output styles for the api view the reference.

Use cases

The three examples: summarizing a page, creating embeddings, and drafting image descriptions.

I'll reuse this small helper to check support and request access:

async function requestModel(model) {
  if (!("models" in navigator)) {
    throw new Error("This browser does not support Web Models.");
  }
  const access = await navigator.models.requestAccess(model);
  if (access.status !== "granted") {
    throw new Error("Model access was not granted.");
  }
}

Summarize page content

Let's add a summary button to a page that already contains an <article> element.

<button id="summarize" type="button">Summarize this article</button>
<p id="summary" role="status"></p>

const summarizeButton = document.querySelector("#summarize");
const summaryOutput = document.querySelector("#summary");
const textModel = "<text-model-id>";

summarizeButton.addEventListener("click", async () => {
  summarizeButton.disabled = true;
  summaryOutput.textContent = "";
  try {
    await requestModel(textModel);
    const article = document.querySelector("article")?.innerText;
    if (!article?.trim()) throw new Error("No article text was found.");
    const result = await navigator.models.generate(textModel, {
      messages: [
        { role: "system", content: "Summarize the supplied article in three short sentences." },
        { role: "user", content: article }
      ],
      maxOutputTokens: 200
    });
    if (result.finishReason !== "stop") {
      throw new Error("The summary did not finish. Try a shorter input or a larger output limit.");
    }
    summaryOutput.textContent = result.data ?? "";
  } catch (error) {
    summaryOutput.textContent = error.message;
  } finally {
    summarizeButton.disabled = false;
  }
});

The app reads its own page and passes the text to the model. The answer is in result.data. finishReason tells us whether it finished or reached a limit.

Create embeddings

Embeddings let us compare text by meaning. A search for "when is the launch?" could find a note that says "the release moved to October."

Here's how to turn a few notes into vectors:

<button id="index-notes" type="button">Create note embeddings</button>
<p id="index-status" role="status"></p>

const indexButton = document.querySelector("#index-notes");
const indexStatus = document.querySelector("#index-status");
const embeddingModel = "<embedding-model-id>";
const notes = [
  { id: 1, text: "The release moved to October." },
  { id: 2, text: "The design review is on Tuesday." },
  { id: 3, text: "Support hours are 9 AM to 5 PM." }
];
let noteIndex;

indexButton.addEventListener("click", async () => {
  indexButton.disabled = true;
  indexStatus.textContent = "";
  try {
    await requestModel(embeddingModel);
    const result = await navigator.models.embed(
      embeddingModel,
      notes.map(note => note.text)
    );
    noteIndex = {
      model: result.model,
      entries: notes.map((note, i) => ({
        ...note,
        vector: result.vectors[i]
      }))
    };
    console.log(noteIndex);
    indexStatus.textContent = `Created embeddings for ${notes.length} notes.`;
  } catch (error) {
    indexStatus.textContent = error.message;
  } finally {
    indexButton.disabled = false;
  }
});

embed() gives us a vector for each note. I've kept the model ID with them because we'll need the same model for search queries.

Accessibility tools

Let's have the model write a first draft of alt text for an image. We'll put it in a text field so the author can edit it before publishing.

I'm asking for a structured response here, so the model needs to support image input and JSON Schema output.

<label for="image-file">Choose an image</label>
<input id="image-file" type="file" accept="image/*">

<label for="image-context">How will this image be used?</label>
<input id="image-context" type="text">
<button id="describe-image" type="button">Draft alt text</button>
<label for="alt-draft">Alt text - review before publishing</label>
<textarea id="alt-draft"></textarea>
<p id="image-status" role="status"></p>

const describeButton = document.querySelector("#describe-image");
const altDraft = document.querySelector("#alt-draft");
const imageStatus = document.querySelector("#image-status");
const visionModel = "<vision-model-id>";

describeButton.addEventListener("click", async () => {
  describeButton.disabled = true;
  altDraft.value = "";
  imageStatus.textContent = "";
  try {
    const image = document.querySelector("#image-file").files[0];
    const context = document.querySelector("#image-context").value;
    if (!image) throw new Error("Choose an image first.");
    if (!context.trim()) throw new Error("Describe how the image will be used.");
    await requestModel(visionModel);
    const result = await navigator.models.generate(visionModel, {
      messages: [{
        role: "user",
        content: [
          { type: "text", text: `Draft concise alt text for this image. Avoid guessing details. Page context: ${context}` },
          { type: "image", image }
        ]
      }],
      output: {
        schema: {
          type: "object",
          properties: { alt: { type: "string" } },
          required: ["alt"],
          additionalProperties: false
        }
      },
      maxOutputTokens: 120
    });
    if (result.finishReason !== "stop") {
      throw new Error("The description did not finish. Try again with a larger output limit.");
    }
    altDraft.value = result.data.alt;
    imageStatus.textContent = "Draft ready for review.";
  } catch (error) {
    imageStatus.textContent = error.message;
  } finally {
    describeButton.disabled = false;
  }
});

The image comes straight from the file picker. Asking for an object with an alt field gives us result.data.alt, with no JSON string to parse.

Other ideas

  • Rewrite selected text in simpler language.
  • Extract fields from a receipt into a structured object.
  • Receipt organizer.
  • Choose a UI component based on generated content.
  • Use tool calls to filter a list or update a form, with the app checking and running each call.
  • Transcribe audio clips.
  • Offline privacy focused text-to-sql data explorer.

Final Thoughts

With this API, I could add these features to a web app without managing model downloads and execution in every project. This is still very much a proposal, but one that I believe is badly needed. If you're interested in helping move this forward, start by reading the explainer and API reference and joining the WICG discussion.

Web Models API — Models belong in every browser.

A proposed browser API for web apps that need a particular open-weight model. People control access; the browser runs it. Join the Web Models API discussion.

webmodels.dev
